NOTICE is Herf,by Givcr' l that the following is a copy of an ORDER which has been made y the Right Honourable Sir Matthew White Ridley, Baronet, M.P., Secretary of State for the Home Department viz:— WILD BIRDS (ENGLAND).
The Wild Bird. Protection (dounty of 'Chester) Order, 1898, Dated 180 February, 1898.

In pur3uanc of the powers conferred upon me by the Wild Birds Protection Act, 1880 to 1896, and upon appli- cation by the County Council of Chester, I hereby make the following Order, which shall apply to the whole of the County of Chester :- 1. This Order may be cited as " The Wild Birds Pro- tection (County of Chester) Order, l 88." _ - -

2. Ttatime during which the killing and taking of wild birdt, -or any of tlipm. is prohibited by the Wild Birds Protection Aet, 1880 (43 anti 44 Vic., cap 35), shall be extended in the CounLy of Chester so as to be from the Ist day of March to tlao 12th day of August in each year. 3. The Act of 1880, as extended by Section 2of this Order, shall apply within the whole of the County of ChestPr t the kestrel and ElPron as if those species were included in the Schedule of that Act.

4. The taking or keling of the following species of birds, namely:—Keig Fisher,Ge et Crested Grebe,Heron, Goldfiech and Owl, shall be prohibited within the whole of the County of Chester during the whole of that period of the year to which the protection of wild birds under the Act of 1880 (as extended by Section 2 of this Order) does not extend. 5. The taking or deetroying of the Eggs of the Owl, the Bittern, the Kingfisher, the Kestrel, the Heron, the Sheldrake,the Dunlin, the Blackheaded Gull,the Common Tern, and the Oyster Catcher, shall be prohibited in the whole of the County of Chester. And I make the following further Order which shall apply within the portion of the Hundred of Wirral eoloured pink on the maps deposited in the Home Office and in the Office of the County Council, and embracing the low-lying lands ana sandhills situate between the estuaries of the Rivers Dee and Mersey of which the boundaries shall commence to the south at a point of the main highway of the County of Chester, 200 yards to the West of the Dock Cottages near the " Docks" Railway Station of the Wirral Railway, run along the main highway to Bidston Village, and then turn in a northerly direction and run to Bidston Railway Station of the same Rail- way, then turn in a westerly direction and run along the Wirral Railway until it reaches ahe Meole Station of such railway, then run along the high- way near to the Meals Railway Station in a northerly direction to the Irish Sea, then on the north along the margin of high-water mark of the Irish Sea to a point at New Brighton where the Yellow Noses join the said Irish Sea, and then run in a southerly direction to "Warren Drive" or road, and along "Warren Drive to the most northerly house and grounds on the west side of such drive then along the western boundary of the houses and premises situate along the western side of such drive or road to a point 100 yards or so from Grove-road, then turning in a westerly direction along the northern boundarics of the houses and premises in Grove-read, Wallasey, until it reaches the Wirral Railway,then turning in a southerly direction along thc Wirral Railway until it reaches the Wallasey Marsh, then along the edge of the marsh in a loutherly direction until it reaches the Poulton Halfpenny Bridge, then turning in a westerly direction on the edge of the said marsh, until it reaches along the edge of the marsh the main highway leading from Poulton to Meols, such parts within the aforeeaid boundaries as are market garden lands and are not coloured in the said maps are excepted from the operation of this Order. 6. The Act of 1880, as extended by Section 2of this Order, shall apply within the above-named area to the following species of birch? : Red-backed Shrike, Whinehat, Spotted Fly-catcher, Sedge Warbler, Blackcap Warbler,Grasshopper Warbler, Wood Warbler. Garden Warbler, Mistle Thrush,Common Bunting, Reed Bunting,Goldfinch, Wheatear, Chiffchaff, Golden-crested Wre-i, Yellow Wagtail, Pied Wagtail, Water Wagtail, Skylark, and Titlark, as if they were in- cluded in the Schedule to the Act of 1880. _
7. The taking or destroying of the Eggs of all Wild Birds shall be prohibited within the above-named area for a period of _five years from the date of this Order.

8. The taking or killing of ALL WILD BIRDS shall be prohibited within the above-named area during the whole of that period of the year to which the protection of wild birds under the Act of 1880 as extended by Section 2 of this order does not extend. 9. The taking or killing of the Gull and the Tern- is prohibited within the Administrative County of Ches- ter during the whole of that period of the year to which the protection of wild birds under the Wild Birds Pro tection Act, 1880 (as extended by Section 2 of this Order) does not. extend.

is reliable. the Humanitarian League is fully justified in its protest but it may be doubted if ther( is much real tortoiseshell in use, or in demand in these days of sub- stitutes which are equally serviceable and attractive. There has been a departure of late in the matter of fabrics used for wedding gowns. White silk, or satin, are now largely dispensed with, and their place taken by crepe do chine, which is draped round the figure in classic folds. Lady Chesterfield's gown—an exquisite creation—proved beyond doubt, that it is an ideal fabric for purposes of drapery, and for girlish brides, it is in- finitely more becoming than the oftimsa trying silk and satin, to which we have clung 60 persistently. Many fashionab!*3 brides are carrying white ivory prayer books with their initials in urFcious stones, the ~late and all particulars of th 2 auspicious, occasion e,n which it is u-,ed being duly inscribed thtireon Chenille embroidery is now very fashiorable, usually being carried out in the same colour as the gown. Em- broidered on net, the effect is very soft and pretty. Tucks are as much en evidence as ever, and appear on sleeves, skirts, fronts, bodices, vests, &c. For cording, the satin cord i 3 nearly always used, and this particular idea nrorniles to be in greater vogue th +la ever thi spring and coming summer. _

div.head: MY DEAR NELLIN,
div.p: MY DEAR NELLIN,

I may at once inform you that ler+t much alters- ation has taken place in the general style of blouses. It is much tucked, and many of its varieties have small square yoke-pieces of lace or—in the case of the thicker silk blouses—of stitched velvet. A more uncommon model, also of silk, has a deep vandyked collar forming a plastron in front, which is edged with fringe. As a rule, this collar is of the same material as the rest of the bodice, but it also looks well in white or ivory Bilk. There are also many pretty fashions of making blouses. I think one I have is very interesting. It is of broadly-tucked silk with an extremely deep yoke (covering the points of the shoulders) oi jewelled net over satin, a style which works out effectively in deep cerisd, with black net embroidered with silver and imitation diamonds. I am informed that ribbons of all kinds will be introduced on gowns as well as blouses this coming season. Shot ribbons, and those that are entirely striped, or striped at the edge and checked in the centre, are being worn largely as well as the more fanciful ones with gauze insertions or edgings of lare.

There are tr:t foe got 4 millinery styles elksut now but 1 think I can describe a couple of charm- ing millinery triumphs well within the capacity of the amateur worker. he first is quite a simple affair, and an example of the present craze for cloth toques. It merely consists of a frame, cue- ningly swathed in three-quarters of a yard (or even lens according to tuze and shape) of violet cl,th of heavy make, such as felt, or the material employed for cycling skirts. It is loosely and apparentiv exrelemly caught up in front, where it is finished with a 6uNtor of violets shading from deepest purple to tenderest mauve, a scheme of colouring destined uequestionably to prove emi- nently becoming to a blerkle. The other would be equally becoming', e.ne:. comiet3 of a felt or velvet hat with a wide circular lJriiu tilted at the one side, and trimmed c5,•...e ostritch feathers and velvet.

There is quite a diversity of ideas about coats, some still prrferring the long threequarters. They appear to have had their clay, and, now that we may soon he expecting bettor weather, we may look owl for a suitable jacket. Short fur coats are extremely modish and charming when relieved with lace chiffon and such-like ethereal fabrics at the neck. An ideal codurne is a soft clinging grey gown worn with a square-out chinchilla coat, and swathed toque of the same delicate fur finished with a chou of purplish crimson, the same colour. ing appearing in the frills of chiffon and silk, finishing the muff with the assistance of a cluster of flowers.

Semi wonderful embroideries are already being stitched upon net with combined straw and floss folk, while what are known as falling flowers, that Is to say, garlands attached to the flimsy back- ground only here and there, are to be a further 'fascination. Made of the softest velvet, of still softer chenille, oc of delicate crepe, with touches of crystal and coloured jewels, these are mag- niflcent adornments, and cost, of course, a great deal of money. In regard to tailor-made gowns, a subject ever varying but always interesting, there is a distinct tendency to do away with the long clinging skirt, and to permit us to use our limbs comfort- ably when we don a walking costume. The tuck- Inge which are introduced on the hips and at the back have a pretty effect, but for a cloth or tweed gown nothing can approach the pleated skirt.

To effect a pretty coiffure the hair is divided is the centre, while a string of pearls encircles the bead, a jewelled pearl ornament resting on the centre of the brow with an almost eastern effect. The deep band of pearls surrounding the throat and fastened at intervals with brilliant slides is also one of the /Smartest arrangements in jewellery, the gli3tening lustre of the pearls enhancing the wearer's claims of beauty, while even the plainest woman seems to derivs a certain amount of beauty from the sparkle aud Rash of diamonds, For those to whom the real artiola is quite unattainable comes comfort, ia the reffiction that an excellent imitation can be easily procured, which will look almost as well, but care should -be taken to select a carefully finished article, as those of inferior make will be easily detected.
Your loving JENNII.
THE MOST NUTRITIOUS.

div.head: CHAPTER XXVIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVIII.

When Ruby arrived at Mrs. Vernon's door it was five o'clock. She had refused food and had not tasted anything since breakfast. The footman stared at her as he opened the door, and Harris, the lady's-maid, came running downstairs scarlet from indignation. -

"Goodness gracious me, Miss Halkett 1 That is the way you treat poor dear Mrs. Vernon! You pretending to be so good and to run off when my poor mistress was at death's door for all you knew 1 But she has heard of your conduct, never fear, and you shall hear how disappointed she was with you. That's the way with young lady upstarts as look so meek; and then when a poor lady, as has been kind to them, being beggars as you might say—why they run off on a spree. Oh, it's shameful! "

Ruby felt too much shaken to defend herself. She crept in and followed the maid into Mrs. Vernon's room. The old lady had recovered with the help of the doctor which Ruby had sent. She was reclining on a sofa in her room. "Here is Miss Halkett," said the maid, tossing her head. "She has had a noice day out when you 'ave been suffering." Mrs. Vernon looked up at Ruby, who was so much bewildered that she did not know what to say. She was quite overdone, but she was too proud to give way before the maid who had tried to insult her.

"Well, you don't look much as if you had en- joyed your day out, Ruby." "I am so sorry, dear Mrs. Vernon, but I- It was not my fault. I cannot say more. Will you believe me ? " "I told you, ma'am, that she would say that." "So you did, Harris. You must feel as if you were a true prophetess. Of course I am disap- pointed in you, Ruby, but lam not fit to talk now. You can go to your room, and I don't want to see you till I have considered the subject. No excuse you can find is good enough to make me forget that you ran away when I might have died." Ruby staggered from the room. Her heart setimed to be breaking. Everything had gone wrong with her, and she felt as if she was the most miserable girl on earth. Alec had never been near her, and her father had forsaken her. She sat with bewildered eyes and clasped hands, wishing that Dr. Murray would come. He would understand and and advise her. But the best would be to see Alec appear. If he knew how much she wanted him, surely he would come. He had said-- Perhaps he had not meant it, and he had forgotten her. It all seemed so sad and so inexplicable. Suddenly she heard steps on the stairs. It was the footman knocking at her door. _

div.head: ‘;-V-h--a-t-i; it ? " she asked, opening her door.
div.p: ‘;-V-h--a-t-i; it ? " she asked, opening her door.
_ "If you please, miss, there is a gentleman downstairs who wants to see you." Ruby's heart beat fast. It must be Alec at last? Her face flushed crimson and she said:
"Where is he ? " "He won't come into the drawing-room, miss; he is in the dining-room." Ruby knew that no one in the house ever went into that room when Mrs. Vernon was ill.

"Thank you. I will go down." "He says that he is in a great hurry and can't wait. He would not let me tell Mrs. Vernon. He only wants to see you for a minute." "I will come down at once," repeated Ruby; but, nevertheless, she ran to the glass to see if her hair was very untidy. "I shall see him alone for a few minutes. 0 Alec, if you knew all I have gone through for your sake," she murmured to herself. Then she ran down the stairs. Her head felt burn- ing, she seemed to be in a fever, but Alec had come at last, she would mind nothing. At the door she paused; through the hall window she saw that a cab was waiting at the door. It made her feel faint and brought the remembrance of another cab waiting for her. Then she opened the door softly and saw someone sitting with his back to it. Alec? No—but it was—yes, it must be—her father! "Papa is it you? Oh!" She was by him in a moment. Her arms were round his neck, and she was kissing him as in the old days before the arrival of the Feltons. The squire rose. He said nothing for a moment. Then he put her a little back from him, and looked at her. _
"Ruby, dear, you are ill! But I have so little time--"

"Papa, what is the matter? Oh, you, too, are changed. You look as if you-4' "Yes, I am altered. I have had- Never mind, Ruby. I want to see you once more as in the old days. You do love me a little in spite of all-"
It was cruel to remind her. Ruby hid her face in her hands.
"I forgot for one minute. 0 papa, how did you find me out? You have not come to take me to- No, I will never go." - _ - .

The squire sat down. He seemed quite unable to stand. "Ruby, can you control yourself? You are al woman now, you have proved it. I was wrong to think that you would be driven. It was all impossible, and now it has been in vain. My poor Ruby, I have been in trouble. lam now, but I wanted to see you once more, to hear you say you forgive me. If that is impossible, at least to see your face once more before going away. I am doing this at the expense of— Listen, I do not know what I am saying, I do not know how to tell you. Since I have been in town I have led a wretched life. I fled from Yewdale to avoid—to-- but here it is the same. I am followed. I don't know why, how it happened, but, Ruby, there is only one way for me. I have thought of the possi- bility of this for years, but now it has come. It was easy for me to give them all the slip, but James gave me your address' and I could not resist it, Ruby. Even if I lost all I felt that I must see you once more, that I must hear you say some- thing, even if it is only that you hate me.' "Papa, what can you mean? I don't under- stand. It is about James. Oh, yes, it was dread- ful, but you did not know all; you could not. He is so wicked. Ile is a bad man, and even for yen I will never be his wife. I would rather die."

"How could I have brought all that on you, Ruby? You are the only creature I have ever loved; but it has been my undoing." "Oh, no, don't say that. It can't be. What is it? I see now it is not your fault. You were obliged to give me to James Felton. You said you could not help it, but even for you I can't—l can't. Papa, give it up. Let us go back to Yew- dale. Tell James that he is never to come near us again. If it is money he wants give it him. We will be poor. God has taken care of me, and, you see, I have found kind friends. You and I will get on without money, papa. Promise me." "0 Ruby, it is not that. It is too late. James has gone; wt least, I think so. Ho ham son. to the station. He told me to come and fetch you. He has arranged everything for you and me to travel with him, but I said I would come here. That would be the last place they would expect to find me." _

"The last place, papal Why? And who are they ? " "Because I must fly, Ruby. Will you come with me and Felton?" "You know I cannot. I will not." "To save me, Ruby. He will, he can, save us, but I could not go without seeing you." . _
- "To go away -with you and J-anaes! Oh, why? I will never be his wife."

Ruby moved a step away. "In half an hour, Ruby, we could be safe. What am I saying? I meant to think only of you. No, I must think of you." "Think of yourself, papa. I don't understand. What is the danger you talk about? Have you lost money? It is all the fault of James, I know." "In half an hour I must leave you. I wanted you, Ruby, but I have no right to haTe you. I have sacrificed you. I -" "I know, I know. But don't go; let James go alone and stay with me. If it is any loss we will be poor together. I do not mind." "It is worse than that. It is-" He seemed suite unable to speak. g Papa, tell me what it is?" "Ruby, tell me once more that you love me, and that you forgive me." "You know I love you. I was sorry, and, eh, so much hurt; but I say to myself You are my father, and you had a right to think that I should obey you.'" "And now," said the squire, looking at her as if he did not see her. "I am nothing: I have nothin.g.

r must fly, if 1 do not want to spend my days in—" Ruby's eyes looked horror-struck. "Papa, you frighten me; don't look like that Whatever people say, I will go with you. You are my father, you have always loved me; I can't help what other people think. I must not mind what you do, only give up the Feltons ; they are bad. Oh, when I read your old letters, I knew that you were brave, and good, and geaerous, and that if you seemed different now, it was because you had to do with bad people. It was not you yourself that—" _Ruby stopped suddenly because, looking at her father, she saw a strange, wild expression come into his eyes. He stretched out his hand, as if he wanted to find some support, and Ruby took his Irembling hand, and held it round her neck. "Papa, lean on me, tell me everything. You will never say that your own daughter forsook you in the time of your trouble." "That my daughter did not forsake me in the time of trouble," he repeated after her. "Yes, papa, no one ever shall say that. You know that 1 was obliged to go because of—that; but now, say you give it up, and we will face the world together. Give James all the money we have, and we will work. I have learnt so much since I have been left alone. But, papa, you may lose everything, but you have still a daughter." "Ruby, you are not my child," he said, slowly, as with a great effort. There was a terrible pause; Ruby's eyes dilated, her whole frame shook; she let her hands fall by her side as if all will-power were forsaking her. A mist floated before her. "I am not your child," she repeated, slowly. "Papa, don't say that—don't." "Ruby, it is true. I might have gone, and never had the pain of telling you; but I—l love you." "You are not my father ? " At this moment there was a sharp ring at the door. A cab had driven up, neither of them had heard it, but they heard the door open and a voice exclaim: "Can I see Miss Ruby at once ? " Ruby seemed to come back to life; she ran to the door and locked it. "You are in trouble," she said. "You said just now that you had to fly. I don't understand. But no one shall say that I betrayed you. What is it? Quick—" "It is too late, Ruby. I had the chance, but I gave it up because I loved you. Let them in, I can still fight for myself, if it's worth the while." The door was tried, Ruby did not know what to do; but in this house she knew that she had not the right to lock a door. She was bewildered, but she made one effort. • "What is it? I am engaged." "A gentleman says he must see you at once." "Ruby, it is Alec; let him see you." Ruby opened the door, and as Alec hurried in he stopped suddenly, and found himself face to face with the man he was wanting. "What do you want ? " asked the squire. "I have only this last hour heard where you were, Ruby. A man Ido not know found me out, and told me to come to you at once, here, as you were in trouble and needed a relation; but I see that you have your father—" "0 Alec, Alec, where have you been? I did want you', but I have been so "long alone, everyone forsook me, and now I'can't understand." "What are you doing here, Sir Harry ? " said Alec, sternly. 'I do not understand all that has taken place in your house; but the man who informed me that Ruby wanted a friend has told me that you—" "What did he tell you ? " said the squire, stand- ing erect and defiant, his old imperious manner returning. "What has anyone told you ? " "I think that before Ruby, before your own daughter, it is hardly seemly to speak of affairs that must pain her." "You can say what you like; Ruby will feel nothing now." "I am sorry that you have no consideration for her; but I must think of her first, even when her own father will not." "Her own father," he repeated. "You can speak." "Yes, her own father. You tried to sell her to an unprincipled man. You wished to force her into a marriage which you knew must mean nothing but misery. You made me sign a will, se that she might be the better worth stealing; you--" "Say what you like about me, but do not dare to say that I did not love her. It is because I love her that I am here and in your power." "In your power, he says. Alec, oh, don't use it I Spare him, even if lam not—" "It is true. Ruby is not my daughter." .g=

• • • • • • • • Dr. Murray and Mr. llansford met on the steps of the doctor's house. "I have bad news, doctor. lam afraid that Felton has escaped entirely, and I have missed your squire by only a minute. Of course, we must get Mr. Beauworth to prosecute, and we must not let him escape." "I have seen young Beauworth. I found him, and I gave him a hint that if he would call and see Miss Ruby Halkett, he would find that she was the same as Miss Ruby Beauworth." "Then he must be with her and he does not know the truth. We ought to have seen him first and to have prepared him. I only hope that this squire will not slip through our fingers as well as Felton." "The best thing for us is to get him into a corner, lie may not show fight. If he holds out, it will be the case of another great trial." "Is there enough known to warrant an arrest ? " "We must see Mr. Beauworth first. If you think that he is at Mrs. Vernon's, will you come with me, and we may get him to take proceedings at once. It is not likely that they will go together." They took a cap, and hurried off to Mrs. Vernon's house, where the footman opened to them. "Is anyone with Miss Ruby P" said Dr. Murray. "Yes, sir, there's two gentlemen with her. I don't think that Mrs. Vernon would like me to let in any more." "Two—who are they ? " "They did not give their names, and it isn't usual for strangers to come here, as you know, sir." The two looked at each other.

"What shall we do ? " "I will stay outside, sir, and will you ask Miss Ruby to speak to you, and I will see that no one goes out." It was at this moment that Ruby found herself in a terrible position. "Cousin Alec, what does it mean? Help mo. He says that I—l--" There was a knock at the door. "If you please, miss, Dr. Murray is here, and wishes to see you alone." Alec went to the door. Ruby placed her hand on his. "No, don't go. Save him—ask him to tell you. I don't know what to think. You will be noble and generous. For my sake, save him." "Go now," said Alec. He opened the door and shut it behind her, and then he turned towards Sir Harry Beauworth, who had sunk on a chair as he gazed at Ruby's retreat- inc figure. Alec came forward.

"Tell me, Sir harry, what you mean by your words. I have a right to know. Through you, if not at your instigation, I have been at death's (-3(ylr ; through you I have suffered more than I conic]. have thought possible." " A 1 aOW is your time of revenge," said the squire, rising, as if some hidden power was giving hint stret:gth for a last struggle. "You can take f,way the one being I love, and you can take away

"For Heaven's sake, do not speak in riddles. I know withing, except that I was most shamefully tre;oed in your house, and that owing to unex- pected help, I: was set free. For all you cared, I mi.:M. have died like a rat in a hole." " \Vas it so? I did not know it," said the R1.17,ir0, indifferently. "Well, I tell you now you yourelf." .\ C 0 overrowaring anger rising within had this man in his power now ; he from him. Ire would unuvis'p: the villainy with which he was concerned ; Ito would brand him as an inhuman father ; he vf•old--- but—what had he said ?—that he was not rAt her? Then whose child was :Ruby? Why 1,1 the squire of Yeivdale adopted a girl who was ii its own, to pass her off as Sir Harry Beau- daughter ? "I< I 1 me, who is Ruby ? The father who owns ,„ay at least he proud of her. She has resisted ha .:= ly,ttn true to herself, though how she I,a agffi is still a secret, to me." • "lquby is not. my &tighter," the squire repeated, if in a divan%
hen tell me the name of her father," "sir Harry Beauworth." "Good Ileave:is ! What do you mean? Who are Ton "

fliosq:;ire 1. Hen his arms, as if determined h onfession. • never have known. \:•Ent away, and 1. now think it is through one of her Low friends that the secret has come out. I thought, when I came here, that she knew it; but for a moment she still believed in me, she still loved me." _ _

"Ruby loves you," murmured Alec. ,"Then she will be true to you. Has she not shewn her determination of character ? " "The determination of a ,Beauworth. Why beat about the bush any longer? The game is up. I am only sorry that the vampire, Felton, is not here. He will escape. He bears a charmed life. Alec Beauworth, you have every reason to hate me. I had every reason to hate you. You stood in the way of Ruby. I had drained the estate for the Feltons. You are the rightful owner of Yewdale ; but now it is hardly worth having—the orange is sucked dry." "It is my inheritance, but where is the right, Sir Harry? lam bewildered." "He is dead long ago. He died in a waterless region in Australia, on one of his wild explorations. I was the only one with him, I knew all his secrets, / planned to take his place, and I should have died a squire of Yewdale if the Feltons could have been bought. But their. greed ruined me and ruined them." _

"You are not Squire Beauworth," muttered Alec, almost unable to grasp the truth. "No, my name does not matter. I took all Harry Beauworth's belongings, and I was able to satisfy the lawyers. So few knew the real man; he was very eccentric." A whole world of thought was rushing through Alec's brain. He was the owner of Yewdale—an impoverished estate which had been robbed by adventurers, but ne of them was this man who had brought up Ruby and--was it possible ?—had loved her. And yet, but for his visit to Ruby, he would have escaped. "And Ruby," he said, "Ruby, why did you— care ? " _ _ .

"Why did I care for her? Why, indeed ! It has been my undoing. If she had not known, she would have gone with me, she would have been with me when-- Beauworth, do what you like. I cared for that child, and for no one else." Now was the time for Alec's revenge, but looking at the man who had wronged him so cruelly—for he had abetted the Feltons—he wondered why he did not seize him there and then, and make him feel the whole fury of his righteous anger. He did not do so, for this was the man whom Ruby loved—who had loved her.

Was there not something nobler than revenge? Was not this man half purged by love? He loved much, there was no pretence about that, though he had not been able to make the sacrifice when it would have been of some use. Revenge—now that it could belong to Alec, now that he could say: "It shall be mine," he paused. He found himself actually thinking of some plan whereby this man could escape from him and from his vengeance. "You must go, you must leave the country at once, before the law can reach you. For Ruby's sake, remember. lam her cousin, I will take care of her."

"I shall go," he said, slowly, as if he did not understand what he was saying, "but I must see Ruby first." Alec was touched by the man's one thought. He had sinned much, but he had loved the little child whom he had wronged so much by passing himself off as her father. "You shall see Ruby again," said Alec.

"WOMEN'S CHAT."

The history of the Queen is the history of the greater part of the nineteenth century, and L- is no less than sixty years ago this month since Her Majesty as married. The ceremony took place in the Chapel Royal, St. James's. *bn February 10th in the year 1840 Dr. Hawley, the Archbishop of Canterbury, officiated, but he died in 1848, avel since then there have been five suc- cessors to the See of Canterbury. Few, in fact, of the distinguished company who were present at the Queen's wedding, still survive. Among these are the Duke of Cambridge and his elder sister the Duchess of Meeklen- burg-Strelitz. The Duke was then not much more than twenty, and his younger sister, the late Duchess of Teck, who was also one of the cempany, was a little girl in short frocks. Since those days, the Queen has had tne satisfaction of seeing the Empire grow and prosper by unexampled strides, whilst personally she is beloved and respected to a degree that has been been rarely, if ever, equalled in history. The Duke of Rutland who was born in the year before the Queen, and whose Parliamentary career is almest synchronal with Her Majesty's reign, has found himself able to take up his residence at his house in Regent's Park, fir the Parliamentary Session. It can scarcely be expected that the Duke will be able to take a very active part in the proceedings of Parliament but happily the House of which be is a member does not find it necessary to conduct debates at enormous length, and does not make the same tax upon the health of i's uaem- kers as the House of Commons. The Duke, it is said, has never been quite the same since the death of his wife, to whom he was devoted. The Duchess was indeed a pattern wife. Simple in her manner,and easily acces- sible, she lived for others, without any show, parade, or fuss. The Queen thoroughly appreciated the Duchess's character and saw much of her when her husband was in attendance in Scotland, or on the Continent. Princess Henry of Piece, who has lately presented her husband .with a much longed for son and heir, is still one of the most beautiful women of our day, with hir lovely, sunshiny face, and magnificent golden hair. To her inexpressible grief, she lost her first little child, but now another has come to fill the void in its mother's heart. There are still rumours to the effect that the ens gagement of the Princess's only sister, Miss Sheiagh Cornwallis West, also a great beauty, to the young Duke of Westminster, is an accemplished fact, but that the betrothal will not receive confirmation until Vets Duke returns from South Africa.

Many a small evening party is enlivened just now, by guessing contests. A sheet is suspended across the room, and through an aperture one nose, or one ear ap- pears, or one eye, or mouth is visible, and guests on the ether side guess to whom it belongs. It is rare indeed that the owner of the eye, mouth, etc., is hit upon, for any one feature of the face, unless extremely prominent is hardly recognisable when taken separately. Prizes are awarded to those who score the most successes, and among millionaire hose and hostesses these not infre- quently take a mest elaborate and costly form. Yet another idea among up-tc-late women, is to have photographs of cane eve only, taken, delicately mounted, and sent direct from the photographers to their friends; who promptly despatch the pictures to the supposed owner thereof. Needless to say these photographs fre- quently accomplish a considerable amount of travelling ere they finally settle down. There has always been some question as to who was the dieetverer of photography, just the same as there is some doubt as to who first produced the lucifer match. There is however no quettion that William Henry Fox Talbot first invented the process of printing from a negative in photography, a preeess which was described to the Royal Society in 1839. Talbot was born in February in the year 1800, and it is now proposed, as a memorial, to raise a fuad for the restoration of the chancel of Lacock Matey, at his borne near Chippeohane. Many years before Talbot begun his experiments, "Sun Pictures" were produced on sensitised paper. Thomas Wedgewrod the son of the fameus potter, pre- clec:d these,in 1802,but the tame most popularly associ- ated with the discovery of photography is Daguerre, echo was a Frenchman. He brought out the dirguerrotype in 1809, the same year as Talbot completed his experi- ments, hence the disputed question of priority. But the two diecoveriea were really quite independent. The duguerratype, as many may know, was a silver plate, covered with a solation.upon whieh the picture was pro- duced and afterwards fixed. Each repetition had to be taken separately. It was Talbot's process which ad- mitted of the taking of any number of photo from a single negative, and to which we really owe the wonder- ful developments of what is probably now one of the most popular of the arts. Tortoiseshell, like jot, has gone very largely out ot fashion but it will surprise most pe pie to learn that this affords another example of cruelty to animals.which is laid to the charge of womankind in procuring its finery. The Humanitarian Leaeue has issued a leaflet on the subject in which it st stes that tbe tortoiseshell from which combs, hairpins, etc., are-made, is obtained by the systematic torture of the animal from which it is taken. According to this authority the shell is taken from the sack of the liyine turtle, whi,h is c -vered with burning charcoal, to facilitate its removal. If the turtle survives, it is allowed to crawl tack to the sea, where it may renlate itself, and possibly afterwards be once mote subjected to this horrible process. If tkis account

div.p: ESTA a L !SHED
CHAPTER XXIX.

There were two doctors round the bed of No. 77 in one of the big London hospitals. A nurse came up to say that there was a visitor waiting to see the patient, if the doctors would allow it. The elder one looked at his companion, who nodded. "No use waiting; ask him to come." In another moment Alec Beauworth stood by the small hospital bed, and stooped over towards the patient. "Bob, Bob," he said, softly, "I've come to see you. Don't you know me ? " The patient opened his eyes and smiled. "Yes, a-course I do. You're Mr. Alec, my— my friend." "Yes, Bob, I'm proud to say it—Bob, my friend." "Thank you. I never had one before, and I didn't expect to have one like you." "You'll have a great many, Bob, when you are well. You must make haste. There's Miss Ruby longing to come to see you and thank you; and there's the kind doctor who came to see you last night and sent me here this morning • and—" 'But father won't be over pleased, Mr. Alec. What's become of the squire ? " Alec hesitated. He could not tell Bob all the story. "The squire was a bad man, Bob, but I hope that he will be sorry for what he did." "He was cute, but I didn't like him, Mr. Alec. You'll tell mother, won't you?" "Yes, and when you are well you will tell her yourself, and you shall live with me, Bob, and I'll work for you. " "That would be queer, Mr. Alec. No, I'll do the work, and I can make the boots shine like any- thing. Why, here in London, they'll take you in even about blacking." "We'll work together then, Bob, and we'll have a fine holiday, you and me and Miss Ruby, and go into the country." "Go on, Mr. Alec, that is fine." Alec's voice was still husky. He was talking at random.

"And we'll go down the liver, and when the day's work is over--" When the day's work is over; yes, that's it," "We'll, we'll--" Alec fairly stopped, and at that moment the door opened and Bob's mother entered, and Alec slipped away outside the door and somehow smothered a sob. "Doctor, is there no chance? I don't want any- thing to be spared. He's a noble fellow." "There's no hope. He was injured internally. I am surprised at his strength; we can but deaden the pain." Half-an-hour later Alec went in again. Already there had come a great change over the patient's face. Bob was beginning to ramble, and his mother was sobbing by his side. "B3b, Bob, say good-bye to your friend," said Alec. _ .
Bob did rouse himself again. "My friend, mother; I've got one. He's :here. He's Mr. Alec. My—friend, who--" That was Bob's last conscious word on earth, but his sentence was finished in Heaven. _
_ Whilst this was going on in a London hospital, another scene was being enacted in another part of London. _ _ .

It was a small lodging. Everything in it was dingy. In a melancholy room a man was sitting in an armchair staring at the fire. His arms were crossed, and his whole figure expressed dejection. Now and then he looked round as if the unfamiliar things about him were displeasing to him, and as if he wished to try and recollect where he was. "What's the use of anything now? It's all gone. Money, place, all that made life worth having. And she is gone. Ruby, Ruby, it was all for your sake, Ruby. I should have been braver and thrown it up long ago and not sacrificed her. I was a beast, and now there's nothing worth living for, nothing. Well, there is one way out of it, anyhow. Better than living on here --" There was a tap at the door and the landlady appeared. "Please, sir, there is someone waiting to see you. May I show them up ? " "I said that I would see no one," he said, roughly. There was a soft footstep, and Ruby stood in the doorway. The landlady disappeared to avoid a scolding, and shut the door behind her. The squire started up. His hand shook convul- sively, then he sank down again in his chair. Had she come to reproach him? "Father," said a soft voice he knew so well. "Ruby, don't—don't you know ? " Then Ruby was by his side, her arms were round his neck as in the old days before she knew, and her cheek was against his,

"Father, you were a father to me, whatever they may say, and I have come back to you. You look so ill, so changed, but you will get better. We will go where no one will know us, and we will work. Honest work must be good, and I know I shall find something to do, and Dr. Murray will help me. Father--" He did not seem to hear, but stared at her as if she were saying something which he could not hear and could not realise. At last he said: "I am too bad for you to have anything to do with, Ruby. Go away, child. Did you come of your own accord, or did they send you ? " "Don't look like that, father. I am not going to be sent away. I will not. We shall live together. You know you said that I was a child. Oh, I am a woman now, you will see." She knelt i bx him.. and took his cold hands n hers an.d

warmed them. "We shall be poor, but that won't matter. You did not think I should mind it, did you? I would rather work for you than live with any rich people." "Have you had the choice, and chosen me, Ruby? And I did all I could to wrong you.", ,1 Ruby put her hand over his mouth. "Hush, we won't say anything more abOuClßel past, but about the future. 0 papa, they hal* all been so good to me, Alec and that kind doctors Papa, you didn't want me to go away with that man? You said you didn't. You couldn't help yourself, and you will like to know that Iswae, helped." "Not now, not now, Ruby. Tell me again that you came here of your own free will." "Of course I did." "But I am a doomed man. You will not be safe with me." "I have thought of all that, papa. We will go away where no one will know us and where no one; will find us, except-" "They will find me out. They will set spies on me." •

"No, they shall not. I will tell Cousin Alec to stop it all. Papa, he is noble. He will never revenge himself, he said so." "He has been very good to me. It was for your sake, Ruby, he found me this shelter. But, Ruby, he is poor; he will have very little money. The Feltons have taken everything. I have made you a beggar, Ruby, and him, too, and I meant to provide for you." "Papa, it is my turn now, I will provide for you. Trust yourself to me."

The righteous are not forsaken. Brave as Ruby was she could not have fought the battle of life alone, but Mrs. Vernon was anxious to shew that she was sorry for having doubted Ruby's gratitude. She had tested her to see if she would give up wealth and ease for a man who had done her a great wrong, and she had not found her wanting. Then she sent for Alec Beauworth, for by this time she had heard all the story from the lips of Arthur Murray. _ _ _

"Come, sit7d-own opposite the light," she said, "and let me see you. You are a Beauworth, and if you are anything like Ruby there must be some good in you." "I could not have done what she has done; She has gone with her pretended father." "And who is going to keep them?" "I shall, if she will let me." "What nonsense! I hear the estate will takd years to recover." , "We must wait for years." "You can't do it, neither can she." "Others have done it." "And you are in love with this mistaken girl ?*,

"I love Ruby with rill my heart." "You are an architect, that is not a very lucrative occupation; besides, you all build houses badly now. "I shall work hard, and I think I shall get on.'l "Well, you had better only give your mind to your work, Sir Alec, till you have unencumbered acres." _

"Thank you, bag shall think first of Ruby." "Indeed you shall not. She is my companion; I shall give her a salary if she will come every morning to me." f; "Will you? Ruby said that you had cast her off."

0 "She deserves it for preferring a vagabond to me; but she understands my cats better than most: people. Pompey misses her too. You can tell her .this from me. We must get something for this vagabond to do or Satan will be finding other mis— chief for him. Of course, he ought to go to prison.",, "I will not prosecute." "I suppose you are a fool and so is she." "I see that you are good and generous. Thank you, in Ruby's name." ; "Don't thank me yet. Good-day to you, and another time don't run into clang's with your eyes shut."

After all, Ruby's path was lightened by the friends that had been raised up for her. It is true she lived in a poor lodging with her father, and that she worked for him with her hands and her brains, but when her labours were over she could *go to the Murrays' house, where Alec was sure to be asked to meet her, and there they would meet for a few hours and be happy. But she did not 'often leave her father, who failed much from the day that he knew that he was being hunted down..., tHis memory failed him, and he would have bursts ,of temper to all who came near him except Ruby,. and with her he was always gentle. If she was 'away he fretted for her, but one word from her, one &ouch, would bring back his contentment. She would find him some copying to do, and he would work hard when she was away, but in her presence he preferred to be idle. He would look at her asi • she busied herself with household things, and that was enough to keep him happy. The summer came and the hot rays tried him, but he would not go away. He felt that in London he was hidden. Ruby's cheeks became pale, for her labours were seldom ended, but she never complained. Mrs. Vernon was always kind, but she, too, got to depend on the girl and to work her hard, and so the busy days went by. t.When the winter came Mrs. Vernon fell ill, and Ruby nursed her tenderly, till one day another • fainting attack came on, and when Dr. Murray came he saw that she would never recover. That evening the end came, and Ruby felt that she had lost her best friend. But the next day Ruby had a surprise. She received a visit from a lawyer,: who informed her that Mrs. Vernon had made her her heiress and that she was now rich. Ruby could hardly believe this strange news. "Has she made any conditions ? " "None. She said she trusted you."

Ruby went to her father. - "Papa, you will get well now. We will go to the country and you need not work again. How good and kind Mrs. Vernon has been. And Alec, he will be glad." To her surprise the squire shook his head. "No, Ruby, I must not touch a penny of it. If it is yours then--" "Then, of course, it is yours, dear," she said, stroking his head. "Then we must give it all to Mr. Beauworth." A blush overspread Ruby's face. "Of course, papa, you are right. It will be your restitution." He nodded his head. "I shall be able to look. him in the face, Ruby, and he will not cast it up against you. Now you will--" "Papa, as if he ever would! But you are right, I will make it all over to Alec as soon as I can." From that day the squire became more contented and less morose. He did not consider whether Alec would accept it or not. He even asked to see Alec, and to humour him they let him and Ruby think this transfer should be made.

So one day Alec, at the request of the man who had nearly been the means of his death, came to see him. They did not say much at first till 2 the squire called Ruby to his side. "Are you still of the same mind, Beauworth, about her? " Alec smiled. "I have never changed."

"Well, now you are in a position. to marry her. Take her, Beauworth, I give you the dearest thing I have." He placed Ruby's hand in that of Alec's, and the two felt that their hardships had not been in vain. All idea of revenge had died away--burnt up in. the nobler feeling of forgiveness.
A year after Ruby's adopted father died with Ruby's hand in his and a smile on his lips. "Ruby, you will go back to the old place," he said. "Think son:etimes of me."
"0 papa, if only you could come, too." "No, no, Ruby. I have been a bad man but you have made me see things differently. God bless you, child, and him."

The bells of _ Yewdale rang merrily one summer day. It was the wedding-day of Squire Beauworth and Miss Ruby. Once more a Beauworth was coming to the old place, and once more there would be good times for the villagers. It was a very quiet wedding, but none the less happy for that. All the Murrays were there, and Dr. Murray gave the bride away. Old Nancy was there in a bright silk dress, and Bob's mother was going to be housekeeper. Happily, for her, her husband had deserted her and the inn was in other hands, but in Yewdale churchyard was Bob's grave, and over his head-stone was written: "Greater love has no man than this." So the bells rang merrily and the people were happy. The old house was hardly recognisable, for all the portion connected with sad times was pulled down or altered. Ruby had insisted on this, and her money had made it possible to free the place from debt, and to ;ina,ke it what it had been in former times, a home for all those who needed help and kindness, a home where love and nob hatred would live till death parted Sir Aleo Beauworth from the lady of his heart. [THE END.

div.head: CONSCRIPTION.
div.p: CONSCRIPTION.
Meeting of the Warrington 'rades and Labour Council.
Lively Discussion.

The menteity meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council was held at the "Waggon and Horses" Inn, Buttermarket-street„ last week. There was a large attendance of delegates. In th- absence of the President, Mr. A. C. Binks, Mr. B:own was unanim- Gusty elected CO the chair. TOE QUESTION OF CONSCRIPTION.—LIVELY DISCUSSION. Toe following circular was read from the Lincoln Trades and Labour Council by the Secretary :—Dear Sir,—At a meeting of the above Council, the following letter was read from one of the delegates :—" Fellow members, I believe our sympathy is with the soldiers of the English and Transvaal armies, who have been ordered to settle a grievance by killing one another. I wonder if we have thought that it might be our lot to be forced into like cenflicts, unless, by agitation we waken the workers up to the real meaning of the Secretary for War's statement (I believe made in the House of Lords), vie " That at some future date he would introduce a Bill to compel each county to raise so malty men for the army ? Surely this means coreicrip- tion. What steps shall we take? Can we be Trade Unionists and Conscripts? Can the Council suggest some actioa to resiit this attempt at Cooscription?" Toe Council decided to lay this question before the Trades Councils of the United Kingdom, asking for an expressien of opinion on the questioa of " Conscription, ' how it will effect the workers, and whether it would be possible to organise a united resistance, should this or any future Government try to fore. " Ooneeription " upon this ceuntry. Shouid your Council pass any resolutioe, or e.ake any suggestion, I should be glad of a copy for future reference. On behalf of the Council, H. DUCEWORTH, president, H. M. Lane, secretary." The matter had previously been before the Council, but the consideration of the letter had been adjeurned to that meeting• The CHAIRMAN said the question was one in which all must have taken a very great inter, .t and he thought it was one of the most important questions that had cern° before the Council for some considerable time. lie asked them to give it their careful consideration and do some- thing practical in face of the attempt that would un- doubtenly be made to force conscription down the throats of working men. If it came about, he-believed that they as fathers of families would regret having children to be nothing more that slaves of the capitalist class of the country. They were asked by the Lincoln Trades Council to formulate some resolution. This had been done by other Trades Councils and he believed there was sufficient interest in the qoeation in Warrington, for the Warrington Trades Council to take the matter

up. Mr. WILCOCKS thought it was unnecessary for the Council to waste much time in considering the matter that night. Lord Sali2bery had made a slatewent re- cently to the House of Peers to the effect that the youngest member of the House would never live to se conscription. In the House of Commons Mr. Chamber- lain had spoken to the effect that considering the altera tion in the mole of modern warfare and the manner in which the volunteers had responded to the country's call he did not see that conscription would ever come to pass in this country because there was no neceoiey for it. Fie (Mr. Wilcocks) thought if they wasted the evening in discussing the question pro and con, it would not be for the hest interest of the Council. Mr. MALKIN was of the same opinion and proposed that the letter lie on the table until the further de- velopment of the question. • MR. GREALY seconded. Mr. STOTT moved an amendment that the Council heartily support the circular frana the Lincoln Trades Council. He thon:ht it was a very important matter. The soldiers had responded nobly up to now but they did not know what the future had in store for them. They did not know how many men would be wanted and how many would volunteer to fight. He was convinced that the workingmen of tbo country did not want anything like the conditions which existed in the French and German armies. If they were going to allow a small body of men to bring them into conflict with the workingmen of other nations he did not think they could call themselves Trade Unionists. He thought it ought to be absolutely optional whether a man Was agreeable to' sell himself." It was nothing moze or less than hiring themselves for murderers. Mr. Meexue : Oh ; rubbish. Mr. Sneer went on to say that if soldiers could be got ty force or voluntarily. the Empire would be extended. Mr. BATTERSBY: Is he right in discussing the ques- tion of extending the Empire. Mr. STOTT: I will give my reasons for moving the resolution. If we allowed a Conscription Bill to be passed we should be in the hands of a few men. Mr. MALKIN : We have no Bill asking this question. When the time arrives that there is a Bill asking f)r it then is our time to oppose it. Mr. STOTT: That is your opinion, I am giving my opinion. The CHAIRMAN : The question is the circular of the Lincoln Council. Mr. BATTERSBY : Does that refer to the extension of the Empire ? The CHAIRMAN : I think so, certainly. Mr. STOTT said that not only the Lincoln Council, but he believed the feeling of the workingmen throughout the country was against conscription. He moved the resolution that they heartily support the circular. Mr. LEM seconded. Mr. Pereisoon said he did not believe it was at all necessary to force conscription on the people of this country. At the present time they knew that volunteers had gladly come forward to try and do their duty and it had not yet been found necessary to force conscription. To his mind the day was far distant when it would be necessary—(hear, hear)—but at the same time when the matter was brought before them, out of respect at all events to the Lincoln Trades Council they ought to deal with it and let them knew their opinion. Hs supported the amendment. He thought that if the Government would, instead of endeavouring to improve the army by conscription, deal more fairly with the widows and orphans of the soldiers,they would not need conscription. They needed army reform more than conscription and if they dealt more honourably with those left behind by the soldiers, they would find that instead of conscription there would be men ready and willing at all times to respond to the call of their country. Mr. BATTERSBY supported the motion that the letter lie on the table. He said that the Lincoln Trades Council seemed a great deal more energetic in political questions than in trade questions. The filesmiths had written to the Council for support on several occasions and had never received any answer, but when it came to a question of picking a hole in the present Govern- ment they were ready to do so. They sent circulars out for that purpose, which cost money, but they could not send a penny to assist the filesmiths when they were on strike. To anticipate a thing of that sort was monstr- ous. Conscription might take place or it might not, but for a Trades Council to take action on the recommenda- tion of men who had taken no active part in Trades Union principles except for political purposes, was decidedly wrong. There was no anticipation of conscription so they should leave it alone until some- thing was done and then consider it. A vote was then taken and 9 voted for the resolution and 12 for the amendment. Mr. BOOTH then moved that a special meeting be held in a fortnight to consider the question. Mr. Meexne seconded. The SECRETARY: What position shall we be in if I write to Lincoln to say we heartily support it and sup- pose at the meeting the resolution was upset? Mr. MALKIN: We do not heartily support it. We are divided in opinion. The Chairman : That is cutting straws altogether. The amendment now becomes the resolution that we heartily support the Lincoln Council. That was carried by 12 votes to 9. Mr. BATTERSBY said he understood that if the amend- ment moved by Mr. Booth was cerried it would do away with the other resolution. The CHAIRMAN : You cannot do that. After some further discussion a vote was taken, 13 voting for the resolution supporting the Lincoln Council and 10 against. Mr. BATTERSBY : And you are going to put the word heartily when it is only carried by 13 to 10; very heartily too. The matter then dropped. THE WIDOWS AND ORPHANS OF SOLDIERS. The following letter from the Blackburn and District Trades and Labour Ceuncil was amongst the correspon- dence read by the secretary :—Baecxnunn AND DISTRICT TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL, 1, Clayton-street, Black- burn, January 1900.—Dear Sir,—At the last general meeting of the above named Council held on Tuesday evening, January 16th, 1900, the following resolution was unanimously carried and I was directed to forward you a copy of same with a request that your Council would adopt a similar resolution and forward Fame to your local members of Parliament " That we the mem- bers of the Blackburn and District Trades and Labour Council, consider that the maintenance of those who now are, and those who may hereafter become depen- dent on public charity through the war at present going on should be undertaken by the State." Your immediate attention to this would greatly oblige, yours on behalf of the above Council, P. Maguire, secretary." Mr. Berreenv moved that the resolution be adopted. Mr. MALKIN seconded, and Mr PLINSTON supported the Motion which was unanimously agreed to. THE PROPOSED CHURCH PARADE. The subject of attending divine service with the Presi- dent on May let was again discussed. On a vote being taken a resolution in favour of attending church was carried by a small majority. It was decided to inform the President of the result of the voting and see whether he took any further action In the matter. TELE END Of THE FILESMITES' STRIKE. div.head: MARGARINE OR BUTTER?
div.p: MARGARINE OR BUTTER?
Some Facts Concerning Substitutes.
Supposing you aiked for a pouud of butter, and a shepman : " On, don't havd lye:ter ; have maNarine. It's just the same thing, or even better, except that tilt) name's different."

Would you take his wo, d for it ? And suppwing that, not cor.tent with ycur refosal.the shopman stid persisted in arguing abon- it, saying, " I understand these things ; you don't. 'she sunstitaite is really just the &tura as too real butter!' What would you think in such a case, and what wool I you do ? You would come to the conclusion that the shopman must have a very low opinion of your intelligence ; you would go away and buy not only your butter, but any- thing else which you warited. elsewhere. In that way you would show that the man made a mistake in think- ing you easy to impose upon. some years ago margarine was packed up very much like roe butter, and labelled with names resambliw' butter; "butter:me," and 30 on, Parliament put a atop to this. You can now distinguish batter from margarine by the label. Margarine, honestly sold as such, i 3 a use- ful article, sad no honest butternaan attempts to sell it as butter.

But apply the same idea to some neterious sutsSitutes. Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people are well known to you. These pills have cured a number ot painful, dangerous, and troublesome diseases amens; your neigh- tours—diseases such as ansemia, St. Vitus' dance, rheu- matism, consumption, paralysis, indigestion. They give new blood to bloodless psople, and new strength to weak people. Supposing you go to a shop and ask for Dr. Williams' pink pills (you should always be careful to ask for Dr. Williams') ; and supposing the shopman offers you something else—a substitute—which he de- clares to be "just as good," or "the same thing," and probably cheaper ; you will be wise to draw the same conclusion as in the case of the man who tried to sell you margarine for butter. The man who tries to sell you a substitute instead of Dr. Williams' pink pills thinks you "simple." He will be persistent ; he will keep on talking about it. He may put the two side by side—the genuine pills and the substisu e—and say, " Look, they are exactly alike !" But they are not exactly alike. There is no resembl- ance between them. Substitutes can never be Dr. Williams' pink pills any more than margarine can be butter. And you can tell the difference by the label, in this case, as in the other. Look for all the seven wonle of the title on a pink package with the name in red, and de not accept any- thing that does not bear th,,,sei words. If the bhopman will insist in trying to make you buy a substitute, go away. Have no more to do with him. He will cheat you in other thinc, besides this, if he finds you so simple as to accept his subitituts in this C 450. The character of substitutes is snowra by everything connected with them. They are often a good deal cheaper than Dr. Williams' pink pills, yet a dishonest shopkeepsr is anxious to sell them. Why ? Because however cheap they are, he can still make more profit by selling useless substitutes made of cm- mon drugs, than by selling the genuine pills. It is herd'y necessary to say mere. But another thing also marks the character of the substitute—the sham pink pills that are not Dr. Williams' pink pills. They are got up to trade on other people's reputation—to sell on the reputation of Dr. Williams' pink pill,. It is not to be expected that goods got up in that spirit will be honest goods ; and, in point of fact, eubstitutes never cured anyone. Dr. Williams' pink pills have cured morn than 27,000 cases. Below is printed one case. If the substitute-rnengers could point to such a cure as this, do you not think they would do so? But they cannot. Sub- stitutes are simply a trick to Sell common drugs. It is only the genuine Dr. Williams' pink pills that really cure, and the following instance is given as one example of the way the pills cure : " Mrs. Hodder, wife of a master builder, residing at the Bungalow, Longlands Park-road, Sidcup,oKent, said to a reporter, who took down her words: "I have been a great sufferer. At times I could do nothing : I could not feed myself. I could not stand. I was, as it were, completely paralysed. From a child I had been a great sufferer from neuralgia which in later years developed into what one doctor termed neuralgic gout and another muscular rheumatism. My doctor felt it was a hopeless cave. Then I consulted a specialist, wno said he had never seen anyone's nerves in a more dreadful state. I was under hie treatment for about ten months, and still suffered. The agony was awful, and I became & perfect skeleton. I could not eat, nor sleep unless I had a sleeping draught. I was as helpless sometimes as a little babe. Mr. Hoddsr wished rate for a beg time to try Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. I had quite given up hopss of recovery,and had said, " I will try nothing else, for where so many remedies had failed, I thought the pills would be of no use. My husband procured a box, how- ever, and I soon began to feel better. I could sieap ssetter, and began to enjoy my food. I continued to take the pills. Before I did not get downstairs for months. I could not stand on my feet. my limbs used to he stiff and swollen, and my hands and fest perfectly rigid, and if you had given me £lOO I could not have moved them. My recovery is entirely due to Dr. Williams' pink pills. I have no doubt of that, because I have been so different since I began to take them. I now take no other medicine, and I would not be without them." To avoid the tiresome talk of substituters the bait plan is to avoid their shops altogether. Go where you are served cheerfully and respectfully with what you ask for. If there is any difficulty, write direct to Dr. Williams Medicine Company, Holborn Viaduct, London, enclosing the price—two shillines and ninepence for one box, or thirteen and nine for sX boxes. But it for any reason you must go to a shop where substitutes are sold, take care to ask for Dr. Wi and see that you get them, with the full name on the label.

div.head: SERVING POLICEMEN WITH
div.p: SERVING POLICEMEN WITH
BEER.
Charge Against a 1/Varringtori Publican.

At the Warrioaton P lic court, •,o Moo ia. , o' ore Mr. Bi:•&?All (in the chair), Council ,r Smethol.3E, :doors. Geddes and S. Wright, Thlma; 80-c)w, landlord of the " Ruzig o' Bells" Ina, Wilderspool Causeway, was charged with having on the 2nd inst., unlawfully sup- plied intoxicating liquor to P.C.'s Bradley and Smith while they were en duty.—Mr. A. Browne represented the defendant. _ _ _

Superintendent Moeaghan (in the absence of the Chief Constable through indisposition), briefly stated the facts of the case; after which he cellee Police-Sergeant Lewis, who stated tied he was on duty in Wilderspeol-road at 4.20 on the afternoon in question for the purpose of visiting P.C.'s Bredley and Smith. He 00111 d not find them anywhere, hut from information which had been supplied to him he watched the prem- ises of the defendant, and eventually saw the policemen leave the back premises of the Ring o' Bells. He spoke to them and then he went inside the house and had a con- versation with the landlord. He asked : "What about these two constablee, Mr. Boscew, who have been in here r' and his reply, after some hesitation, was "Well, Sergeant, it is no use denying it, they were in and they had a drink each,but they did not stop in many minutes. I don't know whether they were on duty or net." In answer to Mr. Browne the Sergeant said be culd not say whether the men had cspes on or not. P.C. Smith (60) said that at 420 he went into the Ring o' Bells beerhouse with P.C. Bradley, and they were Gaol Eupplied with a drink of beer. P.C. Brad'ey paid. Witness was on duty. The landlord did not ask them whetheL they were on duky or not. Witness had since been dealt with by the Watch Committee. Mr. Browne: And the Watch Committee blamed you more than the publican? Witness : Yes' sir. Mr. Browne: And the defendant did not ask whether you were on duty or not ? Didn't you t.AI the Watch Cenerni:tee that you covered your armlets over with yeur capes ? Witness: Yes, sir ; I saw Mr. Boscow look at our arms, but he could not see the armlets. Superintendeet Monaghan : I thought it was P.C. Bradley who told the committee that. Witness : I coincided with his views. _ _

P. 0. Bradley (50) also gave evidence He could say nothing in addition to what Smith had said, they both covered their armlets with their capes, and the landlord did not know they were on duty. By Mr. Browne: Witn.sa had had a " send-off "at the same place a week previously, as be was going to the front, and he knew Mr. Bescow very well. He also stood a friend a glass of beer en the second ;rut. There was no secrecy abeut the matter except that the armlet was covered. He was very sorry the offiace had been committed.

Mr. Browne observed that a publican had no doubt at times difficult duties to perform. and sometimes he might make a little slip, but the question the magis- trates had te put to themselves that morning was whether the defendant knew the officers were on duty. It would be more prudent to ask policemen before sup- plying them if they wen., but he was not compelled to do, and a ease had been decided in the Queen's Bench which covered the present one, namely,that of "Mullins v. Collins." "A c instable being at the time on duty removed his armlet prior to entering appellant's house, and was served with liquor. The Queen's Bench Divi- sion held that a licensed person whs supplied liquor to a constable on duty under the bona-fide belief teat he was not on duty had been guilty of no offence under the acction, and as there was no guilty knowledge or wilful blindness or carelessness which might be constructed into such knowledge quashed the conviction." What were the facts of this case ? The two constables were together, and &meow believing they were off duty served them, as their armlets were concealed by their capes. There was a man in court for whom Bradley also paid for a drink ; in fact be paid for thinks for all the tt Mr Boscow served the men, and received the money and he contended, therefore,that there was no intention to evade the Act. As the defendant was under the bonafide belief that the men were not on duty he was guilty of no offence under the section. There was cer- tainly no guilty knowledge this case. Ho served the constables without asking a question, which he was not bound to do as long as he did not see the armlet. The officers had been brought before the Watch Committee, the Mayor in the obnir,and it was unanimously felt that the constables were more to blame than the publican, and that they had tempted him to commit the offence. He (Mr. Browne) thought this was a perfectly proper case to bring before the Court for two reasons— one reason was that a publican had no right to serve a I policeman while on duty, and the other that officers should not tempt beerhome keepers and publicans to serve them. He thought the justice of the case would be met by the defendant being ordcred to pay the costs. He ought to say that he had kept the house for ten years, and that this was the first case which had been brought against him. Superintendent Monaghan: That is so. The Chairman (after a short consultation with hia colleagues) said the Bench had unanimously come to the conclusion that there was no evidence that the publican in that case knew that he was doing an illegal act or that the policemen were on duty. There- fore, they thought the justice of the case would be met by his payment of the costs. At the same time they thought it very desirable to say that publicans had diffi cult duties ta discharge to keep the law, especially in the ease of policemen who were also guardians of the peace. It Was very bad on the part of the police to tempt publi- cans under circumstances like those. It would be as well if a publican, when a policeman came into his house, would ask distinctly, although the law did not say he should do so, whether he was on duty. Then he would know whom to serve. The ease was then dism'Ased on payvnent of the costs, , 61. Eld.

div.head: SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN BOWLING CLUB.
div.p: SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN BOWLING CLUB.

Annual Meeting, Mr. Walter Brough presided at the annual meeting of the Sankey Bridges Bowling Club, held in the school- room on Saturday evening. The Mayor, who is one of the vice-presidents, and a hearty supporter of the club, wrote stating that be re- gretted his inability to attend,laut aseured the members of his best wishes for the success of the club, and of his interest in it. In his report, the Sscretary, Mr. Highley-reviewed the work of the past year, and congratulated the members on the progress which had been made, and its present state of organizatioe, and, consi lering the necessary heavy expenditure, its present financial eositioia• The matches played by the club also came under notice, the Secretary pointing out that, although not _winning a game away, they succeeded in winning all those played at home, thus proving themselves better in defence than in attack. The several mains held by the club were re- ferred to, as was a medal competition on the League system, which proved very interesting and instructive to the competitors. The Secretary also testified to the good feeling which existed among the members, which, 'ne said, was all the more remarkable when one con- sidered that, although the club was Wesleyan in name and origin, and the bulk of its members were Wesleyans very different shades of religious belief were represented including Church of England, Congregational, Primitive and Independent Methodists, Unitarian, Zte. Surely it spoke well for the sociability bowling engendered that all these religious differences, whiellsometimes created quite antagonistic feeling, were completely sunk in the good fellowship found in trundling the woods. (Ap- plause). The Secretary in commenting upon the report, humorously suggested that as the re-union of the churches had" hung fire" up to the present,they should submit to Mr. H. P. Hughes and his fellow re-unionists the desirability of emulating Sankey Bridges Viresleyan in establishing bowling greens in connection with their churches, as it would be a step towards the fulfilment of the scheme. The secretary's and treasurer's rep srts were unani- mously adopted. The election of officers was then proceeded with, and resulted in all the retiring officials being re-elected, with the exception of Mr W Jennings,whose removal from the town was regretted by all the member% who accorded a special vote of thanks to him for his past services as a member of the committee. The interesting ceremony of presenting gold medals to the winners of tbe competition followed. The first prize a handsome geld medal, presented by Mr Brough, was won by Mr R Sudlner ; second and third prizes, gold medals given by the club, were won by Mr A Foden and Mr T Brough respectively. The wooden spoonist of the competition was awarded a very nice salad spoon and fork, the gift of Mr. Edwardson. • The President spoke of the indebtedness of the Club to their Secretary, Mr. E. Highley, and said that the members had recognised it, sad tpe result was that he had very great pleasure in presenting him with a token of their appreciation of his services, in the shape of a timepiece and barometer, suitably inscribed. (Applause.) Mr. Highley, who WaS evidently surprised, in ack- nowledging the gift, said that, on the spar of the moment he could net think the members sufficiently for the handsome present they had made him. It was evi- dent that the good feeling he had referred to in his report was a reality,and if ever he required an incentive to do his best for the club, their kindness to him that night would have given it. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the ladies who had provided re- freshments concluded a very pleasant gathering.
