THE AFFAIRS OF MR. W. R. EARP.

At the London Benkrup'ce Court, on Thuesday, a sitting wes held before Mr. Registrar Hope for the pub- lic examination of thie debtor, who applied to pass upon eeeroulate -how.ne grog: d b's £',280 , 11d, of which £3,977 10 ie ui s ,cu , arel asee's £197 12a 11d.—In exarnioat)..it by Yo.. r, tinstatit official reaeiver, the debtor wetted tee.: abeut 25 years ago he started in business of a chemic,l manure mennfacturer at Tuns- tall, Staffordshire, and in January, 1873, he failed in the Hanley- County Court, with liabilities £630 13s 24., and assets £524, and obtained his discharge the following ' April. He was unable to state what, if any, divideed had been paid. 116 again continued the business until 1879, with a partner, when he retired, receiving £7OO to go out. Be then, with a capital of about £5OO. started business as a chemical manufacturer at the Elesmere Works, Halton- road, Runcorn, under the style of W R Earp and Co: He also carried on Preston Brook Tannery at Warring ton. He carried on those businesses to June, 1899,when he transferred the business of W R Earp and Co. to a limited company. The capital of tbe company was £20,000, and he was to receive £B,OOO in fully paid shares, and 8,000 shares 100 p lid. Hs was indemnified against the trade debts, £1,342, and to a mortgage to a bank of £2,975. The company really consisted of his son and himself, as it did not go to the public. He denied that it covered the whole of his assets, as he still had the Preston Brook business. That bad always been a success but for the bad debts that he had been unable to get in. e started that business some thirteen years ago. No tanning had been done there for some time, but the stock was being sold from time to time. Within the last four years he reckoned he had lost £6,000 ever the Preston Brook tannery, but in bad debts only. He was interested in the promotion of the Argentine Borax Company. That was promoted at the beginning of the pre' eat year with a capital of £150,090, and went to allotment unon a subscription of £4,000 and an underwriting of £30,000. It was true that the underwriting contract was not carried. His connection with that company was owing to the difficulty he experi- enced in getting borax products for his factory, owing to the monopoly of a company just then formed. He and his friends subscribed for over 2,000 shares in the company, in addition to which he had accommodation bill transactions with Mr. Arthur Cohen. the promoter of the Company, of which he acted as a director. The bills represented £2,400, and Mr. Arthur Cohen having disappeared, he was called upon to meet them. To that liability he mainly attributed his failure. He admitted I that he had been drawing at the rate of £lO a week 1 from his businese,and that he was overdrawn with Earp and Company, Limited. That was in connection with unpaid fees as a director.—The examination was ordered to be concluded.

div.head: DEEP KEEL OF SOLID GOLD.
div.p: THE DEEP KEEL OF SOLID GOLD.

Attached to the keel of a certain racing yacht is a elab of load weighing more than ninety tons—twenty tons in excess of the weight of the body of the yacht itself. This prodigious counter-balance enables her to carry her immense spre id of sail even in a stiff wind.

But this slab of lead is a big one, and the boat has got to drag it through the water exactly as she drags her rudder. If it were only half as la,rgo, and just as heavy, the yacht wsuld probably win every race she entered for.

Some day, if the yachting rivalry doesn't die out a man may turn up rich enfaugh to replace the lead kee with a solid gold one; then all the cups and trophies will be swept into his net. For, bulk for bulk, gold is nearly twice as heavy as lead.

But he will have to be nicely off financially, and " a dead ganae sport ;" as,while the ninety tons of lead costs only about £2,000, the ninety tons of gold tot up at the snug total of about £1,500,000; at which figure he could build at least a pair of steamships like the Oceanic. With men, as with railing vessels,it is much the same. The light hull, the high propeliing power, the deep, heavy ballast—these things do the trick. The free and agile intellect, the body unencumbered by extra flesh or by disease, the thorough and steady digestion ; human beings built this way sail round the stake boat first and gather in the glory and the prizes—no matter how the wind blows—whether ahead,aheatn, or astern ; pointing, reaching, or running. "For more years than I like to look back at," says a woman, "I was almost croshod by indigestion. After every meal I had dreadful pain in the stomach and chest. Food seemed to turn to acid within me and gave me only slight nourifihment. I had no real rest or comfort day or night. "I could do practically no work, and was of small use to myself or to anyone. I used te fancy nobody could be worse off than I was and still be counted as a living person. Doctors tried their best to help me, but succeeded no further than to procure me an hour of comparative ease now and then I was at last completely cured by Mother Seigel's Syrup. Now any fond agrees with me, and life is a different matter altogether. I only wish it were in my power to impress the value of this remedy upon the minds of the multitude of dyspeptics one sees everywhere in England Perhaps my letter may do eornething towards it."—Mrs Elizabeth Potter, Turf and Feather Cottage, Risley Calcheth, near Warrington, July 28, 1899. For indigestion, dyspepsia, liver and kidney disorders nervous troubles, impure blood, and all those physical disabilities which cause men and women to get beaten in the Life Race, Mother Seigel's Syrup is the thing. It
stands for the great sails and for the Deep Keel of Solid Gold.
"Robert Louis Stevenson."

This was the subject of a paper read at the meet- ing of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society on Monday evening. The President (the Rev. Morley Stevenson) said he was sorry the weather had obviously thinned the audience. The fall of snow was the greatest which had eccurred in Warrington since the year 1881. He well re- raembered the time, because he had just come to Warrington, and was getting into his house when the snow came, so that it made a great impression upon his mind. Notwithstanding the inclement weather, Mr. Gow bad come all the way from Leicester to lecture to them, and they regretted they had not a better muster to present ,to him. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. Henry Gow, of Leicester, then read his paper. Stevenson, he said,was a great artist in words—one of their greatest, but the special charm of his writings, apart from style, might, he thought,he expressed in language similar to that of Matthew Arnold by saying that he was the friend of those who wanted to live heroically in the) body, of, all who loved a pure, healthy, breezy life, who enjoy simple travel and hard exercise, delighted in adventure, and wished to make the commonest life adventurous and heroic, even the sick bed. The five senses and the pos- sibility they offered to romantic treatment, of beautiful and wholesome enjoyment were con- stantly the note of Stevenson's writings, and the power when the body was weak el, overcoming and lising still heroic:illy, and finding joy in the senses that were left . that was the note one felt in Stevenson Ile was an invalid from the time of early manhood with constant threatenings and mutterings of death in his ears,and they gave him some of the hardiness and the philosophy of the soldier; he treated sick- ness as Columbus treated storms. It was all in the day's work to be met with indomnitable courage and hopefulness. Stevenson's writings, although the work of a man constantly ill, living always at the very brink of death during the last 20 years of his life, were entirely opposed to the literature of woe; and problems of society did not exist for him; he had other things to do. His books, whatever might be the final judgment and their influence on the future, should be in the hands of all parents and guardians. He treated evil and sorrow almost in a spirit of welcome, while in sickness and poverty he demonstrated the liveableness of life.—The President after alluding in complimentary terms to the lecturer said he ought to state that it was due to the kind suggestion of the Rev W H Drummond that they had had the pleasure of listening to Mr Gow that evening. (Applause.) In proposing a vote of thanks to Mr Gow the Rev W H Drummond said the influence of Stevenson's writings was to quicken one a sense of wonder and admiration and courage in the most ordinary experiences of life.— Councillor Monks seconded and said he had known Mr Gow personally for a long time. It was a great pleasure to see him in Warrington, and his only regret was that there had not been a larger attend- ance to listen to the excellent paper that had been given. (Hear, hear,)—Mr S Kenyon, Mr Thomas May, and Mr G Carruthers supported the motion which was heartily agreed to.

AT MO tiMe we used to The " New" Member. hear a good deal of the

_ _ _ "cross-bench mind." If little has been written on the topic of late, it has been because the type of member who used to sit on the cross-benches has disappeared. tis a rule, these benches are empty except on important nights, when they are occupied by members who do not take an independent view of public ques- tions, but who have no recognised places in the House of Commons, and do not attend with punc- tilious regularity. Sir CHARLES HAMOND has often been an occupant of the cross-benches, but he has usually voted with the Government. Mr. COURTNEY represents something of the cross- bench mind, though he is committed to some causes which prevent our calling him a thoroughly independent member. There are also members who usually sit on one side and vote on the other. Mr. G. 'WHITELEY was a characteristic type of this kind until he was driven to change sides because he had altered his opinions. Sir MICHAEL FOSTER, the new member for London University, now appears in quite a n3w char- acter. He is not certain upon which side of the House he will sit. But his views about the war are of a nature to compel him to take one side, and so he has said that "he should take his sea::, at all events at first, among the supporters of the Government." Hereafter he leaves us to infer. when questions of education or of civil and re- ligious liberty come up, 13.2 will sit on the other side. We have ventured to style a politician of this kind the "new" member. There has been no member of this kind in the House of Commons for some time. Perhaps it has not been possible for him to appear. The University representative, according to the theory whereby such bodies are permitted to return representatives, ought always to be a non-party man. As we pointed out some time ago, the recent University M.P.'s have always been party men. Lord AVEBURY, whom Sir M. FosTzu succeeds, was a party man. The effort to be otherwise has been so impossible that most members have given it up altogether. Accord- ingly, we shall watch the career of the new member with interest. He may be found habitually sitting on the Ministerial side and occasionally voting with the Liberals. Or he may be logical, and indulge in occasional transmigration, making a Conservative speech from the Ministerial side, and a Liberal speech from the Opposition side. If he can consistently act in this way, he will be one of the most remarkable additions made to Parlia- ment in the lifetime of the oldest member. The effort will certainly be considerable, and his obedience to counsels of perfection will not be given without more searchings of heart than are common in these days. He will pardon us if we express a doubt as to his ability to persevere in this exalted line of conduct. We shall find him disposed to take more Conservative than Liberal views, and he will probably discover that if he is to be inde- pendent, surveying all questions from a non-party standpoint, he will have to exert himself so often, to be in doubt so frequently, that he will waver, vote Conservative, or decline to vote at all. Habitual association with one ski° in politics tends to reduce initiative and independence. Still, if Sir. M. Foster should be intellectual, conscientious and industrious enough to give unbiassed vote, upon some critical occasions, he will have set as noble example we should be delighted to see others imitate, and especially University M.P.'s. If they would all make up their minds to sit on the crosz- benches, to sit together, and occasionally to vote together, we should learn to have some respect for the intellect of the wise and the good sense of members oVithe liberal profession. The " new" member looks like a portent. Alas we are very much afraid of the descent to the commonplace.

We have more confidence in the navy than we have in the army, and that assurance is well placed. But in the strategic defence which ;s finding increasing favour the navy ceases to be our [ protection, and we are invited to contemplate a vague scheme in which the ; [ ,-,Ty disappears, and [ leaves our coasts defenceless. oramercial ports, to boalbar3. them, perhaps to overpower them, and to land troops whose advance w"1 have to be repelled by riflemen. To be able Lc --r.c! or coast defences one of two things must, hov,. hanoened—either our ships of War must be engaged on other duties than the immediate defence of our csasts, or they must have been beaten. Now, we have always believed that our navy was large and efficient enough to protect us from invasion, and to meet an enemy in the open sea, or, if necessary, seal up his ships in their harbours. If we are wrong on this point, the country will receive a very severe shock, and the best thing that can happen is that we should at once take the necessary measures to realise the national ideal. Our fleet must be made strong enough to do the duty which the country has as- signed to it, as well as to embark on offensive mea- sures. We cannot accept a theory which starts with the assumption that the Channel and the Mediter- ranean fleets must combine and guard the Straits of Gibraltar, and demonstrate hard by, leaving our shores defenceless for the time being except by coast defences, and swarms of rifle- men on land. Nor can we, except in some general precautionary sense, assume that our fleet has been beaten, and that the supreme effort to guard against invasion will have to

be made by our domestic force, with the regular army, as a mobile force, to deal with an enterpris- ing enemy who has managed to beat U 3 at sea,and land 50,000 or 100,000 men. Whenever our fleet has been thoroughly beaten by a superior naval force, unless that force has been terribly crippled 14 the effort, an invasion may ba easier than we imagine. Command of the; sea being gone, our *bores would be open at too many points to admit of successful resistance to a determined and numerically superior foe, with nothing to fear from ships of war in its rEir. We need not new discuss the possibility of getting transport for a gigantic army of invasion. We are dealing with the theory of strategic defence, and we unhesita- tingly say that it is unsound, and that the country sill be alarmed as soon as it clearly realises that the navy is pronounced insufficient to take an active primary part in repelling invasion because of duties to be discharged elsewhere. To be secure 70 must have a fleet on the sea effectively guard- ing our coasts, as well as a fleet to assume the aggressive miles away. The point is of importance, and the public needs to instruct itself on the sub- ject.

The Queen's summons to Bugler Dunn is a re- Ininder of the intense interest which her Majesty la taking in the sufferers from the war. This brave youth has now recovered from his wounds, and joined the depot at Portsmouth ; but the Queen does not forget that he was the first to be wounded in the Battle of Coleus°, and that he was Particularly courageous because, on account of his tender years, the officers had wished to keep him back. Only a few clays since the Queen stood god- Mother to the child of a Major in the Gordon highlanders, born a few days after the cicer's death, and this sympathy with the Widowed mother will touch the hearts of many Others in this country. There can be no doubt that the Queen, who was most anxious her reign should close without this bleodsherl, has been exerting herself greatly to mitigate the sorrows of her i People. Of course, much of her correspondence s done under general instructions, but quite a num- ber of the letters wiiici appear in the Press bear Clear indications oi her individuality. It is not generally known that the signing of state docu- ments frBquently oo.mpies the Sovereign for three hours a day, and when the consideration of the host of smaller matters is added, end the social function also considered, it will be seen that the Queen is setting an ex-ruplo to her subjects in re- gard to Lard work, her age being taken into calcu- lation.

The Papal rejoinder to the s?irited protest of English Catholics aninst the anti-British senti- ments that dominato the Vatic in will repay care- ful study. It is, in effect, a blast against Patriotism. EiNgish Catli4)lics must not presume to be patriotic sae ail the independence of their country come into conflict with the "independence and liberty necessary to the Church." They are exhorted to sacrifice their love of country, to wit- ness its danger and ruin unmoved, if by so doing t. hey can exalt the power ot Rome. Happily, there is little chance either of Catholic or Protestant Englishmen being compelled to witness our national downfall; but in the task of avoiding that calamity it is useful to know the sentimentsof those rho think they might benefit by it if the event faPPened. Ecclesiastical Rome is, as always, in- tnsely hostile to England. The hate is traditional. "e have managed to survive it since the Armada, and t.here is no reason to fear it now. It may bes„rtf alulY make mischief for us in France some day it— What the poison cannot do is to sap our irrhength by provoking internal discord. The 4raninotane scheme to detach English Catholics t_r in their country is hopeless. Even a good Catholic does not venerate Rome or Roman methods so much as that. He has his views on ftle malice and imbecility in which ecclesiastical °till is so fertile, and if he does not express them _with Indecorous loudness,he signifies their presence bY the unmistakable candour of his acts when the needs of the times call upon him to do so. Abject Servility to Rorne,such as the Ultramontanes insist upon, is not traditionary among English Catholics.

The conscription bogey has not, as far as we can see, caused much uneasiness or alarm among the male inhabitants of the country; consequently a telegram from New York of Wednesday's date is difficult to understand and at the same time open ,to doubt. The telegraphic message in question states that the Oceanic on that date brought from England 494 steerage passengers,of whom 300 were youths. And these youths, on being questioned, are said to have stated that they left home be- cause they feared the British Government intended to enforce compulsory service in South Africa. They are further credited with the remark that they were only the forerunners of .a general exodus of Young men who were unwilling. to undergo con- scription. The story is certaiul v remarkable, true o. r untrue. Probably there would be no difficulty lo finding 300 young men in this country anxious to avoid conscription, bifc, that such a number B.hould rush ou board one American-bound vessel 18 'fore than we can credit. One of the press „ ic).rri_espondents makes the statement in all good ;t" however, so ho ought to be enlightened. mere. , ino " t-reneral exodus of young men" im- Pen'lng• Conscription has only been mentioned— n.ever seriously considered—and we refuse to be- lieve that any such corps of cowards has left the country in the manner suggested.

Our citizen soldiers who have been accepted for active service in `4e ith Africa now know the date of their departure for the Cape and no doubt many them are eagerly looking forward to the 22nd Lnstant when they will leave the shores of Old t;rigland behind them and set their faces towards the enemy. The date of their departure will Probably be a red letter day in their history for never again in the course of their career may they be called upon to leave their fatherland for a similar purpose. We move quickly in the present day. We can almost imagine the look of pity which ally individual would have evoked, who, cal paying a visit, say to the last brigade camp at Conway, had had the terneriV to state that before the next Years encampment, many of the volunteers before him would have fought side by side with the British Army six thousand miles away from home. And yet that is the spectacle we are witnessing to-41ay. The wonder is that most people take it as matter of course, They are filled with pleasur- able excitement at the scene and admire the loyalty and devotion of the Volunteers, and yet the novelty and uniqueness of the event doss not

seem to strike them. It is, however, one of the facts which no historian will seize as of the greatest import2mcn, and an unexampled illustra- tion of the reserve force behind the British nation. In bidding adieu to the sixty or seventy citizens of this town who have voluntarily taken up arms everyone will wish them God speed.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

The weather has now the adpearance of breaking up, and a gc-•ol taw has set in; so that, in a short time the cinals and roadways, which have been blocked by floe ice and drift snow, will soon be again negociable. Then too, the workingmen of the district, who Imre to depend for their livelihood upon what outdoor work they can obtain, will be able to go back t work and accomplish that which the interv_ntion 02 the frost compelled them to re- linquish. The fact that the Manchester Ship Canal has been kept free and navigable, is, undoubtedly, due to the indefatigabie labours of Captain barley, and his numerous assis, anr,s ; for, notwithstanding the severe frost, the lock; at Eascham and else- where along the vast waterway have been kept workable and tlmo2t entirely free from ice.

Liverpool contemplates a far more stringent watch upon its milk supply, and with that purpose in view the authorities have set their minds upon furthering what is loP,ally described as "the Liver- pool Corporation Milk Supply Bill." The bill chiefly relates to the vexed question of tuberculosis; and aims at a more stringent examination of stock and milk which are in any way connected with the sources of the Li verp)ol milk supply. Whilst the objects of the bill may do much for Liverpool, it is pleasing to see that the Runcorn Rural District Council, at any rate, is endeavouring to do its duty to Cheshire agriculturalists; not only by studying the bill, but by gleaning the views of other Rural District Councils in the County, as well as the views of the County's most reprosentative agricul- tural authorities.

The proposed Transporter Bridge across the Mersey, was discussed by the Widnes Town Council at their Quarterly "Sleeting, on Tuesday last. The decision arrivyi at was an important one, and was to the effect that " the construction of the pro- posed Transporter Bridge between Widnes and Runcorn-road, be a great public advantage; whera- fore, they cordially supported the Bill now before Parlisment." Of course the Council have stuck out for conditional clauses for the protection of the Borough, and got at least definite promises of them. We have now two of the four Councils in favour of it, (and the principal ones too),so it will not be long before the great " aerial ,flight " will be in full swing. RUNCORN S-IDJL BOARD PRIZES.

(1). The pr;zes are net acid never nave been given by "Tie School Authorities." Nut one penny has ever been contributed from rie school funds. The prize scheme was started abut 10 years aeo,and since the commence- ment some £7O or £BO have been raised by means of entertainments, lectures, etc., arid distributed to the scholars in the form of prizes. The prize fund is entirely and absolutely maihesieci by veluntary effort on the part of the teachers, (2). The b ioks awarded at the last prize distribution in December were not" The resultant of an enterprizing firee's advertising acumen," as stated in the "Examiner" notee. Eveier b )ok was bought and paid for. The sum at the dispeeel of the teachers for the purchase o?. prizes amounted °al, to £2—the proceeds of an entertainment. There would have beee a lareer s‘igi, had it not been that considerabie ceeributions have been made to the war fund, the sneoiars' prize fund suffering in conse- quence. (3.) At th,; leet prize distribution ab nit 80 books were purchased with ;he £2, at prices varying from 4d to 2s. They were carefully selected hy the Head Teacher, many of theme beleg Standard works. (4) The prizes were not offered and never have been offered as"a Cull end sufficient reward for regular attend- ance,diligence and success," bile simply as an enco nage- ment to the eehelare to do their best. The pupils are frequently reenindei by the teachers that the best prize they can wig is the prize of knowledee: (5). The prizes have fully served thee purpose for which they were intended, arid as far as our knowledge goes, the reeepienti have invariably been pleased and satiafiA.
(6). The priz? scheml ha l played an itnplrtant part in helping to bring the school to it pre3ent state of efficiency.
(1). The doscription of the prize scheme in the " Ex- aminer" as" a rnkery and a raJostnisity " is nothiag less than a libel on the teachers and the school. "A CORRESPONDENT'S " REPLY.
(1). The Runcnrn Public, and !myself, are quite aware of the working of the prizs scheme, which has the sanction of the School Authorities.

(2). The books which I speak about, could have been purchased for qd. or lees only from a firm who kept the " enecial line " for advertising purposes, there- fore they are " the resultant of an enterprising firm's advertising aeuinen." I accept the explanation abtut the £2, and ho inability of getting a larger sum owing to the calla for contributions to War Funds. But that fewer and bitter prizes could and ought to have been given, is still my ophaion. (3). Simply proves that lam corrert in my "findings of fact "; b )oks at 411 must have been purchased— (and even cheaper ones)—and given as priz.s. (4). lan very glad to bear it ; anti so too will be the general public. But the words " for regularity,diligence. and success "are inside.

(5), There is a oifferonce of opinion upon this point or my informants would never have complained. I how- ever, accept the : " as far as our knowledge goes." (6). No rioubt it hat!, but the public will assuredly see that the "prizs schema" would oring the schools into still greater efficiency, if prizes more difficult to obtain and of better value wore given.

(7). As to "the d,”criptien of the prize scheme in the Examiner" there was none, nor have I ever nublished one. But what I describe as a" monstrosity in conaec- tion with the recent distribution of prizes to the scholars." is pat what it is and nothing else. As for a "libel on the telzhers and the seheol" I simply discharge my duty to the public aud expose where I think there should be exposure and commend where I think com- mendation is earned ; and at the same time libel no one, and repudiate any insinuation against the teachers and staff.

SUDDEN DEATH OF CAPTAIN PETER BROWN..

Intelligence reach d Runcorn, on Wednesday afternoon, of the sud Jen death of Captain Peter Brown, seventy years of age, whilst he was cross- ing the Channel from Belfast to Fleetwood on board the ttoyal Mail steamer Duke of York. De- ceased was a well known and respected Runcorn and Liverpool mariner. He was in charge of a schooner bound from Belfast to Annan, but feeling unwell had decided not to make the trip. Captain Brown resided in Hope-street, Runcorn, and leaves a family of six. MERSEY NIISSION TO SEAMEN. _ _

On Saturday, a little girl named Sarah Birch, aged 7 years, 24, Pear street, Widnes, was admitted to the Accident Hospital suffering from scalds on both legs and arms, caused throuo a pan of boil- ing water being overturned upon her. Dr. Hutchin- son attended her, and her condition is slightly im- proved.—A labourer named Samuel Killeen, residing in Warrington road, Widnes, was following his em- ployment at Tharsis Works en Monday, when by borne means he fed into a tank of copper liquor. The ambulance conveyance was immediately sum- moned, and the unfortunate man was taken to the Accident Hospital. Here he received every atten- tion at the hands of the nursing staff and Dr. Hutchinson, It was found that he was suffering from very severe scalds to the legs, the right side of the body and face. 1.0.G.T. CONSOLATION LC,DGE, WIDNES:

A public meeting of the above order was held in Gospel Union Mission Hall, West-street, Widnes,last Friday evening Mr A Francis, of St. Helens, pre- sided over a good attendanee.—Mr. Jacklin, agent for the order, addressed the company on the temper- ance question. Taking his subject, from an economic point of view he contrasted the log; of life and the expenditure of money in the present war with the less of life and expenditure of money in connection with the drink traffic, and showed how small the war item was in comparison with the other. A programme of vocal and instrumental music was gone through,the following taking part :—Misses C Widdows and L Ashton; Mrs Greenwood; Messrs J Hosker and B. Smith. The accompanist was Miss Tracey. The Farnworth team which has been passed by the committee of the N.C.C.C.A. for competition in the Northern Senior Cross-country Championskip, to be decided en Saturday is as follows :—J Hosker, If Fallow, R Ratcliffa, W Lightfoot, J A Cadman, W H Jones, E Broome, A Haynes, P Brady. J Willis, P Flynn, and T Houghton. Reserves; W Lewis, F Andrews, and M Handley. Owing to the heavy snowstorm the Runcorn Harriers were unable to engage in their usual spin on Saturday. The fixture for Saturday is a most interesting one, viz., the Northern championship, which will be contested at Rotherham Racecourse. Four hundred of the 13..5t runners in the north will compete. The Runcorn team is as follows :—W Thomas (captain), W Ray, S Hopkins, R Redfield, J Goodall, A Casson, J Hill, H Jones, T Shallcross ; reserves R Hamilton, J H Hamilton, and J Austin. The course is well adapted , for the race.
WIDNES ToWN COUNCIL, AND THIII PROPOSEP NEW BRIDGE OVER TILE MERSEY,

The monthly meeting of this council was held at Widnes Town fiall.on Tuesday afternoon., the Mayor (Alderman G I Neil) in the chair. A deputation of the promoters of the Widnes and Runcorn Bridge Bill, 1900, consisting of Mr. Alsop (solicitor) and Mr. J T Wood (engineer,) attended and interviewed the committee with reference to the proposed bridge, and tie committee resolved that, in the opinion of the Town Council, the construction of thOroposed transporter bridge between Widnes and Runeorn would be a great public advantage, and that they cordially supported the Bill now be- fell) Parliament, subject to such clauses being inserted as the council considered necessary for the protection of the interests ot the borough, and the mayor and other members of the council be au- thorised, if required, to give evidence in favour of the Bill before the parliamentary committee.— Alderman W W Gossage, in proposing the adoption of the minutes said the proposed bridge over the Mersey wits of the utmost importance, both to Widnes and Runcorn, opening out the trade of the borough, and,as the company were prepared to con- cede everything affecting their interests, they wished to give them every support. The recom- mendations were unanimously adopted.

div.head: Runcorn Contractor Sued.
div.p: A Runcorn Contractor Sued.

At the Vittint,s County C,turL F:ida) o,r -‘4, he- for# his Itttioue Julge J i.tie Pet,;l Wido w and Anuie Percival,daughter at the late Willtain Percival who was kilted by falling off a scaffold erected in the construction of a new building in the yard of Messrs Bowman and Company, chemical :nanufacturers, Hiechinson-street, claimed £2BO Hs for cempensatien, as dependants of the deceased, from John Garner, con- trictor, alton-ruad, Runcorn.—Mr. M. V. D'Arcy, barrister (instructed by Me. C. El. Lewin), appeared for the p:aintaff, and Dr. Tatatna,l, b tz rister, represeated the respondent.

Mr. D'Arcy said the application was one under the Workmen's Compensation Act of 1897. In answer to the particulars which had been for werded to rep nidea..; giving the usual notice as to name, place of business, and emplayment, the respondent had put in answers as follows : —(1) Tnat the deceased was not employed by him as alleged; (2) that he was not engaged on the work at the time of the accident; and (3) that the respondent was not an undertaker in the meaning of the said Act, and was not liable to pay compentJation. On December 7th the deceased man was engaged on a building which was being canstructed on the prtnises of Messrs Bow- man and Company, and was 30 feet 8 inches in height. Dr. l'hornas :—I admit that the building was over 30 feet your honour. Mr. D'Arey, continuing, said the deceased went on to the scaffold at 7.15 a.m. The scaffold was erected by the workmen of the respondent. At eight o'clock James Garner, brother of the respondent, who was in the employ of the company, teld the man that it had gone eight o'clock ; the bell had rung. The deceased -vas getting down the ladder, there being an interval between the top and the scaffold, when he fell, and Gar- ner turned round and saw the unfortunate man on the ground, three feet from the ladder. He died, and an inquest was subsequently held. The deceased was in the employment of, and had ev)rkeil for the respondent for a period of 14 months, and his wages were 36a. per week. That write(' out would give the amount of the claim. He (Mr. D'Arce) would show that the deceased was employed slide by, paid by, and engaged by the respondent, who to all knowledge was bedding or constructing the building. That brought hint to the hoint as to wkat constituted an undertaker In section 7 sob-section 2of the Act wouid be found a definition. He did not think that this point as to " un- dertaker" had ever been raised before. Undertaker io the case of railcays meant railway companies. In the case of building if it was laid down as the person under- taking for construction, repair, or demolition. He hoed to show that the respondent was an uudertaker withie the meaning of the Act.
Henry nireiyal, son of the threasvl, said his father was employed as a bricksetter at Messrs. Bowman's. Mr. John Garner paid him his wages. H.s mother was old And not able to work.

James Garner, brother of the respondent. Fail the deceased was engaged on a brick wall as a bricklayer, The building was being constructed en the premises of Messrs. Bowman. ells brother found the men and paid them ; the firm did not. His brothel's men put no the sea 'fold.—Cross-examined by Dr. Thomas : Witness was empleyed by Messrs. Bowman, and paid by them, fie was engaged as foreman bricklayer, and the men were under his supervision. fie inspected the scaffold to see if it WAS properly constructed. When the men came to the end of the job it was he who told them what work they should go on with. If a man was not doing his work prioperly he would see his brother (the respondent). The men kept their own time sk-ets, and thee handed them to witness, who took them to the foreman of the yard for him to sign. The latter had nothing whatever to do with the blasts.

Christopher Taylor, secretary for Messrs. Bowman, sail that at the time of the man's fall th-re was a build- ing being c ms:ructod on the firm's premises. 'racy found all material, and the labour was provided by the rospondent. The firm had nothing whatever to do with the eagagemeLt of William Percival. They paid the respesndent's accounts for suoplyinz, the labour. A verbal arrangement was entered Into by witness and Garner Cro3s-examincd by Dr. Thomas: John Garner was not responsible for the way in which the work was per- formal ; that was under their own supervision. Respon- dent had no option himself of deciding how many men would be required ; that was done by the direction of Bowman and Company. James Garner had formerly been a foreman for the respondent. The agreement he made wi:h John Garner at the works was that they should like him to supply the Is hour for the new works they were commencing. He was to have commission on each man's work. This concluded the plaintiff's case.

The respondent said the agreement was as stated by the last witness. He (wirness) had no control of the men at their work, nor any right to interfere with what they had to dn. If something went wrong with the workmen James Garner, his brother, ha I no power to dismiss them. He rnuld nct suspend or atop a man with- out his (respondent's) orders.—Cross-exansined by Mr. D'Arcy, respondent admitted that he engaged the men and paid them. 'Dr. Thomas said he had three points to submit. The first was that the tirn• for the suspension of work had arrived, and it was after the bell had rung,that the man fell from mite scaffold. Secondly, was the man employed by the respondent, and thirdly w.ids the respondent an undertaker.
Hie Honour : It teem; to be an unusual case. I neiver heard of such a cage before.

Dr. Thomas : Whatever t'ae state of things it, it seems to me that seeing what ft, respondent had to do Bowman'i were the undenakers in this case. Mr. ChziE- tap'aur Taylor had told them what the contract with the respondent comprised. He was to find labour for the brickwork as required by them. That was the limit of his obligation. They had been told that he had no con- trol or right of direction, and that he was not respon- sible for the manner in which the work was performed. He submitted n these fasts that respondent was an agent to find the men for the real ensp'oyer. Thu re- possibility for the whole work was Bowman's. There was no agreement between 13,wman and Company and the respmdent bY which they could compel him to execute the building properly. He had not undertaken. He submitted that be could not be held responsible unless he was an undertaker within the rneanicg of section 7. An employcr was not necessatily an undertaker, and the latter on'y was till responsibh p trty un ior t:Io Act. Mr. D'Arcy replied to the legal points submitted by Dr. Thomas,- after which his Honour raid be would re- serve his judgment.
JUDGMENT SUMMONSES.
Important Alterations by Judge Gwynne-James.

Shortly after the commencement of the business at the Warrington County Court on Thursday morning, Judge Garynnf--Jain. s. the recen.ly appointed Judge for the Circuit said he should lika to say in rderence to the judgment summoeses that ha intended to make an alteration in reiereace to the manner in which he should deal wich them. Up to the present it had been customary to make an order of committal for 36 days, that committal to remain in the office and not to issue if tie-3 total amount due was paid wizhin three monthe. Now the result of that ordet was that in nine cases out of tea a person wno gets a judgment against him need I not pay any of the amount for four or five months. A. creditor naturally did not wish to hastily take a judgment out againit kis debtor, but give him a month, say, or two mont 13. If he did not pay, then be was brought forward on a judgment summons and given another thr,e months before he paid a penny. He saw no reacion in Warrington why anyone who was not disposed to pay should pay any debt for which judgment had been given in court before four or five mouths. In future leo intended as a rule, to make an order of 7, 14, or 21 days, or more, as the case might be, and to order that the warrant do not issue for the arrest of the individual on payment of moneys by instalment. For instance,if he saw there was 16s due on a judgment summons, he should order a committal for 14 days,and then order that the warrant do not issue against the indivi Wel if Ito paid regular certain instalments which 11,, should order him to pay. He might order 23 a fort- night, as he had done in the case just heard, or he might order 4s a meath. By that means the creditor would obtain more of his money, at all events sooner, than he otherwise would have done, and the other way would be easier for the particular debtor to pay if he paid by smaller initalments than being called upon to pay large ones. He should be glad if those in Court would make known what he had statei to their friends.

div.head: RUNCORN PIANO DISPUTE.
div.p: THE RUNCORN PIANO DISPUTE.
New Trial Ordered.

On NVednesday, before Justices Channell and Bucknill, in the Queen's Bench Division, areurn, nts were resumed in the case of Crane and Sons v. Holmes on appeal from the Cheshire County Court judge at Runcorn. This was an appeal by the plaintiffs against a judgment in favour of the defendant under these circumetances. Piaintff, a Liverpool firmoet a piano value £45 to Mr. Do Korte, of the George Inn, Runcorn, on the hire purchase system. He went away in October, 1899, be- ing considerably in arrears with the instalment. Defendant Holmes took possession of the George Inn, with everything in it, and he allowed a Mrs. Browning to t. ke the piano way, as she allege De Korte had previously sold it t.) her for £l6. The ques- tion now was whether the defeldant Holmes was liable to plaintiffs for the value of the piano, as they alleged they were the rightful owners under the hiring agree- ment until all the instalments had been paid. The County Court judge found in favour of defendant. Mr. Pickford, Q.C., and Mr. Norridga aopeared for plaintiffs in support of the appeal, and Mr. J. Eldon Henkel for defendant.

Mr. Banks submitted the County Court juige was right. In order to establish a wroag,rul conversion the act complained of must be an interfereace or dealing with or doing some act in negation of ths title of the true owner, or something inconsistent with the right of the true owner, Here the only act relied on as wrong- ful convarsion h 7 defendant was the statement of Holmes that al! the things in the house wore his. That was not asserting a right inconsistent with the right of the true Owner.
kf'er further argument, their Lordthips said the facts did not seem sufficiently clear ; therefore the only thing they could do was to send baek the case for a new trill, costs to abide the event.

Whilst following their employmelt at the Central Station goods yard,on vVednesday dMrning two men met with accidents which necessitated their speedy removal to the Infirmary. One, W illiam Corcoran (39), al, School-brow, was running with a truck when he slipped and broke his leg. This event took place on Tnesday evening in the Co-operative Hall. Sankey-street. A large number sat down to tea, which was on the tables at six o'clock, various lady members of the congregation presiding. At eight o'clock an entertainment was held Mr W J Forshaw in the chair. The Vicar of the parish (the Rev E C E Carleton), Mrs Carletons and the Eev H R Wild were amongst the audience. Au attractive programme was submitted, Mr Vercy Raudall oifi iattn7, as accompanist. The first item was a violin solo, " Selection from the Geisha," by Miss May Jones. Miss Dorothy Trus- love was heard to advantage in her song, and for one so young she acquitted herself remarkably well, having the honour of a well-deserved encore. Mr Leonard Aukland earnod hearty plaudits for his skilful rendering of" The Bugler,' after which Miss Gallaway contributed with effect "La Serenata,' with violin obligato by Mr Fred Randall, both dis- playing no little skill. A praiseworthy interpreta- tion was given of the quartette "Shepherd of souls" by Messrs Woods, Mather, Parr and Aukland, and Mr H M Ashton amused the audience by a reading, in which, as usual, he displayed great elocutionary ability. The fire, part of the programme was con- cluded with a coons' song and dance by Miss Arline Harrison, which was admirably performed. During the interval the Vicar delivered an address. NEGLECT OF CHILDREN.—A ktOTHE'I SENT TO GAOL.— John McLoughlin and Mary MeGoughlin, of Jockey-street were summoned for neglecting their four children on vaeious dates daring the last eix months.—Mr Browne prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P C.C. He said that the defendents were charged with neglecting their four children but the attention of the Bench would be more particularly called to the boy Patrick for this reason. The boy was suffering f,om a dis- eased hip which without any possible doubt was the result of neglect on the part of the parents to pro- cure medical attendance. So far back as April last year. the female derendent took the boy to the Infirmary and Dr. liewden. who saw him, advised her to allow him to remain there. He offered to find him a bed and she promised to take hi el there on a future occesion. The doctor never heard anything else of the boy till hie attention was called to him by Inspector Hackett on the Bla December. The Inspector had visited the house on the 22nd September and had toid the mother that the child must have medicel atten- tion. She promised to take him to the Infirmary, and let him remain there. On the 14th October the Inseector again went in the house but found the defendants had removed. He went to the Infirmary hut the child was not there. He afterwards discovered that they were living at 32, JockeTstreet, and proceeded the-e. Ere found the child was just in the same cendltian as before,and weld not bear Ur put its foot to the ground. Dr. Bowden was called in and insisted on the boy's removal to the Infirmary. The hey was taken there and had remained since the 19th December. He had undergone an operation, but his condition was no better. and he would be maimed for life- He would have to undergo another operation before he could walk, and one leg would always be shorter than the other. The other children were not properly clot had. The total amount of wages corning into the house was 26s.—Bviderice bearing out this statement was given, from which it would appear that the woman was more to blame than the man on account of her drunken habits.—The female def- relent was committed to pal for a month, and the else against the man was adjourned for a month.

ALLrGED PERM i-rTING DNxNiSS AT EtTNCoRN. Jamas Taylor, landlord of the Vine Hotel, Runcorn, was charged with perrnitt,ne dlunkenness on his licensed pre- Raises on he 2nd of February. 1900.—Mr Fleteher (solicitor, liorthwich) prosecuted for the police, and Mr Knowles (soli- tor Widnes), defended.—Mr Fletcher said the facts of the

case lay in a very small compass. They referred to the con- dition of a boatmen named Jaen Twigg. whom it would be shown was on the Premises o: the Vine Hotel from 530 until 11 p.m., with the exception of a short period when he went across the road to get his hair cut and a shave at the barber's. When he entered the house he had upon his person 325. Subseqaently he WAR found lying drunk in the yard of the Vine Hotel by a Police-Constable. It would be shown that he had only El 6s 6d upon his person when seserchei at the Police otation. There WAS a sum of 5s •6d which, it was reaeonede to presume, he had spent upon the premises. Furthermore it wanld be abundantly proved that the man was drunk for he woe afterwards brought before that B.nch and fined. There were the broad facts that at 5.30 the man was sober ;he entered the Vine Hotel, and was drinking there almost all the time ; and was finally picked up in the yard of the place, in a drunken state conveyed to the Police Station and ultimately convicted. Evidence !la support of the solicitor's statement, was given by Elizabeth Twigg. 3oba Twigg (boatpeople),Constable °Arrington and J Wilding. —l.le Knowles, for the defense, assumed that the Bench was English enough not to commit on suspicion, and were he unable to answer the case that would be sufficient he thought to secure It 3 dismissal for there was nothing but suspicion, There was only the word of Mr. and Mrs. Twigg. and opposed to that he ven- tured to think he had two witnesses in Mr. and Mrs. Shakeshaft (lsoatpeople) every bit as respectable. and they would come forward and tell the Bench that Twigg left the public-house at the same time as themselves, apparently quite sober. It was quite possible then for the man to have gone to any other public-house. He would also produce evi- dence to show that all the drink that Twigg was served with while in the " Vine Hotel " was three glasses of whisky and one bottle of ginger beer. Further perhaps, their Worehips had noticed; the man Twigg's appearance, and from his face he would jadge that it would require a man with a long pocket to make him the worse for drink. (Laughter.)—Twigg (from the body of the court) : " I've a face the same as thine." (Increased laugher.) Evidence for the defence was given by Charles Snakeshaft, Sarah Ellen Shalceshaft Ruth Clare (barmaid),John Leyland, Ann lane Parrott (Crewe) and the defendant James Taylor. —The Beach dismissed the case, on the grounds of there being insufficient evidence to convict.

SOCIAL AT ST:.CIETON HEAT.—OD Monday evening the second soeial of the seaeon orgtnised by the ladies connected with the Stockton Heath Choral Society took place in the Institute, and was very successful The building was appropriately decorated. Between 70 and 80 ladies and t entlemen were present, and in addition to an excellent programme of dance music, played admir- ably by Mr. George Lomas, songs were efficiently ren- dered by Mrs Worrell, Miis Rubarts, Mss Shaw, Mr Mason, Miss Budge. .kliss Faulkner, Miss MounDeld, Mr J C Shaw and Mr Whitehouse. Toe .C's were Messrs Worrali and J Shaw, and the refreshment department was in the hands of the ladle? committee. Hughes, who congratulated the meeting upon the good attead ince, spoke of the interest shown in the Band of Hope movement at the present time, and expressed a desire that the Society would become a great power for good in the district. An excellent programme had been provided ,which was neuele enjoyed by old astd young alike. Recitations were very creditably given by the following membeis :—May leherwood, Emily Bond. S E Whitfield, M Bartel], Jane Houghton, Joseph Whitfield, fl Moores, B Isuerwood, W Batten, J Istjrwood, Arthur Whitfield (encored), L Ishenrood and J J Worrell. Mr Ereest Grounds was very successful in his interpretation of "There is a Flag that Floats," and his efforts were reinch appreciated. Mr G WWtfield ably recited." Toe Fire- man's Wedding," and in response to an enthusiastic encore centributed a humorous recitation in the Lanca- shire dialect. div.head: EXAMINER, URIDAY, FEBRUARY 16, 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, URIDAY, FEBRUARY 16, 1900.
NEWTON-IN-MAKERFIELD FREE CHURCH COUNCIL.

In connection with the above a Conversazione was held in the Lecture f1i..11 of the Wesleyan Chapel, Earles town on Wedneiday evening. There were about 100' people present. and refreshments were handed rouna• The Rev. T 11 Law, secretary of the Federation of Free Church Councils, was present, and gave a short address on the objects and work of the council, and also gave lucid answers to several questions which were put to

Later on a public meeting was held in the Wesleyan Chapel. The Rei. F. E Miller, president of the Council occupied the chair aid he was supported on the plat- form by the Revs F a LAW, E Socock, T. PASSMOre, Jas. Allatt and Mr T Ormand. The chairman said there would now be in the future what perhaps there had not been in the past, one voice. 'There was the heart,thevoice,not if msny churches, but of one church, and that voice was being raised louder and more imperatively. teaa it had been in the past. They were able to speak more pewerfully than ever they did, and set forth their plea fir liberty. They were free from State control, but perhaps they realised mere than some of them had done, that they had an object lesson set before them by what was called the State Church. -

They were free from Priestly rule, their churches were churches of free men, based upon the principle that the individual member of one church l claimed dominance over the censcrence of another. (Applause.) ATho Rev. T. H. Law said they had beard a great deal of recent years of Jubilees and Centenaries,but they were there that night to discuss a movement which had barely run its first chapter, 34:1 ho felt hold to say that from that hour it woul be reoegnised as one of the most divins d.svelopments of the 19sh century. They were not there to suggest a new thing in the matter of union, in the priaciVe ot it,it was as old as the New Testament. What was urging them in the churches to-day wee how this union of sentiment could be turned to practical effect. He was there simply to spell out the union, which some of them beliewd in the name of God and by the hrep of the Spirit would do something to solve the rest proble.n. Their movement was one for large owne. He did not knew whether they fully eeeenieed the fact that they lived in an age of large towns- 150 years ago when John Wealey Ives doing his great work it was a land of villages, there wa set a:town in Eneland worth calling a town. But now nearly all the population of England lived in large towns. Disorganised norocoefermity was utterly pewerleiis to deal with the ever iricreaeing heathenism in the large towns of England. There was more heathenism in Liverpool and Manchester than there was in any city to China. How were they to deal with the organised devilry of our large towns, but by organising them- nem'. He had no idea that they were going ts have in hie time one groat ecclesiastical syseue end he was net geing to advecete it, if they had such a thing it would be burdensome. He thanked God that all the largo towns in England were caunin,g into hue, and the grand old man of Lancashire, Dr. Maclaren was renewing his youth over the movement. He did not think Dr. Madera', during the whole of his ministry had: thrown himself so entirely into any movement as he had done la that, and it was astonishing how the movement had grown, as nearly every town in Engeind had a Council. It yens a movement for the towns, and all evangelicel churches we:e coming in, and it was a movernerst also for the villaees. Their brethren in the rural districts were face to fec,e with a hard fight, and they were simply unable to hold their own against sacercletalism ;:ncl territ Jialism. Landlordism and the tyranny of Pr4lii!i,m, if their movezent vrot properly worked were deemed from that day forward. Their mevement meant real business. It was not a mutual Stelitiiratiols society ; it was not a machinery for passing resolutions, nor a tea drinking movement. They were not coming together for the sake of annihilating their denominations. He was not there to advocate that they should Tenet up or level dews, but the Free Church movement was one of the most legitimate movements this country had ever known. (Appl3use.) On the eaetion of the Rev. James Allatt, secluded by Mr. Orrneed, a vote of thanks was acearded the speaker. A siveilar cempliment was paid the Chairman and the Meeting closed.

div.head: TWENTIETH CENTURY
div.p: TWENTIETH CENTURY
FUNDS.
Meetings at Warrington.
Baptist.

Following in the wake of the Wesleyan Methodists anti the Congregationalieta with their 20th Century fanda, the Baptists have determined to follow suit and an effort is being made to raise a quarter of a million sterling be- fore the end of 1901 for denominational purposes. The scheme has been onthasiastically taken up in this dis- trict which his five Baptist churches in its midst and the promises of contributions total up to £250. This is cog- ' sidered highly satisfactory a,nd the conference and meet- ing held in Golborne-street Chapel on Tu?sday will give a fillip to the movem-int. Thn doh- ference opened at four o'clock ant representa- tives were present from G olborae-strolt. Warrington, Hill Cliffs, Latchford, Little L.igh, and Miiton (Acton I Bridge). The Rev. J. T. Schofield presided and he was accompanied within the coinnauni.on rails by the Rev W Cuff, of Shoredi, eta Tahernacl, and vice-president of the Baptist Union • Rv F Iler, of EtArdrONa ; Ray J S Hulloes (Hill Cliffs), Rev J F Matthews (Latchford),and Rev John Aldis (Little Leigh). The CHAIRSUN said his first duty was to welcome, on behalf of heir own church and the associated churches the Rev. W. Cuff to Warrington. They were glad to see him and to know that he was one of those ministers who was willing to address small as well as laree gather- ings and williiig to take a stand besides the Baptists in places where they were weak as well as strong. (Hear, hear.) He (the speaker) was in the fullest sympathy with the object of the meeting that afternoon. He felt that the objects to which the fund was to be allotted were worthy of the support of every true Baptist. Apart from the amount of the money which would be obtained and the objects te which it would be devoted, the very effort of getting the money, the sacrifices it would entail, and the lookir.g up to God would be a great hlessing to the churches. It would bring their churches chseer to- gether. Ever since he had been a Baptist be had longed to see more denominationalism amongst them. They I bad vindicated ther independency by having isolated churches, and he did not see why individual churches could not unite together for the evengelise- tion of the world and the spread of their principles. I He had met Bapt;st ministers and members of Baptist churches whrere B getist principles seemed to carry them no further than their own church. That ought not to be. They ought to desire the spread of the Baptist de- nomination throughout the world. Without under-rating other denominations he thought the Baptist de- nomination was the one nearest the truth. They had not met togteher to inaugerate the 20th century scheme for Warrington and district. They had already started it 6nd they had met to encourage one another in the work.

div.head: REPORTS,
div.p: THE REPORTS,

The CHAIRMAN proceeded to repor; upon what had been done in connection with the Golberne-street Baptist Church. PrOMis, s had been made t 3 contrfl-eito £I.B to the fund, and £26 13s 61 had been paid and forwarded to headquarters. Applause.) The Rev. J. S. HronEs (Hill Cliffe) observed that £6O waa promised by his congregation at the first meeting held to consider the subject. More money had since been promised, and he thought they might possibly raise £BO or £lOO. (Applause.) The Rev. J. F. MATTHEWS (Latchford) alluded to the great effort made to raise money by the bazaar held a short time ago. They made the business "hum," as the Ameiieans said, but notwithstaz dine the great effort then put forth They hoped to raise £5O to the century fund. (Hea , bear.) The Rev. J. ALDIS (Little Leigh) said their resources were not half what they were years ago, but they hoped to raise at leaet £2O. They had already £ll 10s Oi promised. (Applause.) Mr. W. BOUGIE (Milton, Acton Bridge) stated that although the Baptists in the district he represented bad recently built a church at a cost of nearly £1,200,it had been decided to take up the matter of the 20th century • fund and de the best they °Nfld.
ADDRESS Hir THE TICE-PRESIDENT OF THE UNION. THE OBJECTS OF THE FUND.

The Rev. W. CUFF, who had a cordial reception, ad it was a pleasure to him to know that the poor churches were taking up the matter of the fund; it would not cost the rich a single soeeze, they had the money and they could melte it, and there were members of Baptist churches in large towns who had net only got together thousands of pounds but who had thousands a year coming in. The richer churches did give the money, he was pleased to say, but he was still better pleased to know that the small churches were (IOW?, Clo— the churches who lived in perpetual battle from year to year. (Hear, hear.) The Wesleyans were trying to raise a million euineas, the Congregatiocalists half a million, and the Baptists a quarter of a million. What a grand total the three would make. It made the united effort a national one—much wider than any other of the denominations or all of them put together. Such a large sum of money could not be raised for God without affecting the moral condition ot the people of England, the intellectual and religious condition, too. He would be one of the last men in the world to undervalue the force for good which the British Press was. The pen of the pressmen wieldee a power in the daily paper, the monthly magazine, and the quarterly magazine that very few of them could estimate, but he ventured to say that the Press would agree with him, when he said that with at his power if the intellectual forces of the churches were excluled, er were to cease. England would be poverte-stricken in intellectual educa- tion, for the pulpit and the Church wielded a tremend- eus influence on the national life. The irreligion of the people of England was one of the most painful things thoughtful men had to grapple with. Wee-king men had turned their backs on the churches and chapels, and he deplored the frantic and sensational efforts of some of the churches to get working men within their doors. He did not like to name the things that were being done,the unsatisfyine craze for entertainment amongst young people which was killing the life of the best churches, and eating up the blood and sinew and brain of the best. These sensational el_ments wers the signs of the condi- tion to which they had fallen. Praceeding to explain to what uses the money would be put, he remarked that £30,000 would be set aside to assist the weaker churches in the maintenance of their pastors, and £30,000 for the Annuity Fund for the aged ministers and the widows of ministers. This fund would provide for the aged ministers £45 or £5O per year, which would relieve the church deacons. There would be £6,000 set apart for the establishment of scholarships open to any stisdent studying for the-ministry, and £25,000 was to be reserved for educatienal and ether purposes. A boy having received an education at an elementary school would be enabled to go to a higher school, where he would receive a thorough commercial education, when his parents could not afford to pay for a secondery edu- cation. The outcome of these two objects would be that the Baptists would have ministers who had received a university education, which they were often told they did not then possess. £34,000 would be devoted to the erection of a Baptist Church house in London, in which the provincial ministers might stay during their visits, and where the May meetings would be held. In that house there would be an hotel, reading rooms &c. Needless to say, all the £125,000 would be invested, and would realise at least 3 per cent. (Applause.) A number of questions were asked and the Press was thanked for their services. Tea was afterwards partaken ef in the sehoelroom. nee EVENING MEZTING•

There was a large attendance at the meeting held later in the evening, and presided over by Mr. J. Longland. The CHAIRMAN in the course of an interesting address, said that the five ehurebestcennected with the Hill Cliffe sub-district of the Lanchshire and Cheshire Union had made a 20% Century Food appeal, and he had no doubt they had decided how much they would raise, but there were always certain elements that they could act reckon with, and he dared say many of them when they made up their minds as to how much they would be prepared to give did n ,t quite realiz3 what an influesce the speeches made that evening would have upon then,. (Hear, hear.) He had no doubt the result would be an increase of the amouot to be promised, and they would then have double reason to congratnlete themselves upon the fact that they had with them the vice-president of the Baptiet Union. (Hear, hear.) He was under the impression that the Lancashire neePle did not see'enough of the " big lights" of their denomi- nation. If Lancashire was properly looked after there was relenty of ground to cultivate,and he was sure there would be a good return from it. They would be glad to see their friend Mr. Cuff in Warrington again, when he occupied a still higher position in the denomination than at the present moment. (Hear, hear.) He had heard several &ejections to the 20,th Century Fund. Some did no see why they should subscribe to a fund that was going to be scent in the coming years, but he thought they must have forgotten what their forefathere had done for them in gaining religious liberty, especially in the country districts. (Hear, hear.) In many country districts the Baptists and Congregationalists were for a great number of years the only bodies who were represented there,out

aide the Established Church. The Wesleya,ns of course came later. He could name quite a number of places where if it had not been for the Baptists and Cenere,ga- tionalists the people must have looked entirely to the Established Church for their religious instruation. The Established Churn did not altogther answer to the re- quirements of every'oody. He had little doubt that the money whip it wss inten led to raise by the Baptist denomination would be spent in a pro- per and judicious manner. He was greatly in sympathy with the movement for providing pensions for aged ministers Their ministers had many claims upon teem and it was impossible for them to provide against old ace. Ha did not think they can d begrudge the sum of £30,000 Whin it was proposed to devote to that object.(Hear,hearl. He di.l not think there would be mush difficulty in raising half a niillina if the Baptists w ould put their heart into the work.He would like to see Lancaehire standing higher in the list of subecribers Lean at the pr,ts,mt time. Yorkshire he noticed was considerably higher and he dil not think there ought to be that diff t.enee between the two counties. Lancashire Relined to be only just geting te work in the moymient but he had little douht that they would be nearer the top of the fist at,the close. (Applause). Toe Rev. J. 11. ATKINsoN said the fund was worthy of every supp)rt. People thought the poor Baptists couid not raise aqe arter of a million. Bat it could and would be done. (Rear, hear.) it was unique in their history and the fund was net merely for the propagation of their religious principles as a denomination ; it was rather f3r the inceeasing of their denominational unity and therefore their usefulness. There were numerous division 3 among the B aptiste,b3t this fund was brineing them torther. He never knew the Baptists to be so united as they were at the present time. Tnere was great necessity for more evangelical work ; there W 4.9 never a greater need for the teach- ing of the gospel of Jesus Christ. One aim and the chief aim wis that £125,090 was to be soent in evaneelical work. I,: for nothing else, he maintained that that alone made the appeal worthy of their most intense support. After referring to the great difference of opinion in ' regard to the war in South Africa, he said there had ' been nothing more thrilling in their time than the patriotism and generosity which the war had evoked. The people had given abundantly, and men of all ranks had volunteered for service. They (the Baptists) were else engaged in a war about which there could be no doubt as to its righteousness. (Hear' hear.) They were fighting against iniquity, and evil of every kind. They had for their commander one who never had to retreat. 'lney were called to fight under His banner, and if they went forth in His name He would lead them from vic- tory to soctory, gaining pesition after position, and at la3t wsuld conquer the world. (An, lause:) The Rev. W. Cure in the Course of an eloquent address said when Me history of Baptism came to be written this 20th Century effort would be regarded as one of the greatest things accomplished, and that would be something, for they had no mean history, and it would take na small thing to rise to the level of heir glorious forefathers and the church of the early days. There were brains and blood upon every page of their history for which they might thank God and take cour- age. (Hear, hear.) Their forefathers were high-minded men, and bravely gave their lives for their belief. They were meta of personal cenvictien. They would be worthy sons of worthy sires if they showed the coming genera- tions what they thought of those who had gone before. , The Reptists always led the van in Eneland of liberty and freedom and the uplifting of the people. There were times in their history when few men cared to stand for those principles. It was unpopular. But the men of their denomination knew they bad truth at tbeq. side. They had the courage of their con- victions, end the people of to-day had entered into the glorious free lone that they fought for. With the money they were appealing for they hoped to usher in a better Eneland than tkat of to-clar, when liberty would have its proper place, and they would all come to their own house of prayer in which to offer worship to their God. He felt ceri*ain that their nation had even a greater future than they had witneAsed in the past. .He ntust say that in this part of the country they had done splendidly, and if similar generosity prevailed every. where there would be much more than a quarter of a million raised. div.head: EASTERN CUSTOMS.
div.p: EASTERN CUSTOMS.
Interesting Lecture at Warrington.

A lecture, illustrative of the manners and customs of the East was delivered in Bold-street Wesleyan School- room, Warrington, on Monday evening by the Rev. red Lamb, of Wigan. Notwithstanding the very un- favourable weather, there was a fairly good attendance. Mr. J. Taylor preeided and introduced the lecturer with a few well chosen remarks. A number of ladies and gentlemen appeared in costumes to represent various Eastern characters aid their dress was fully described by the lecturer. At the outset, the LECTURER said the object of his address was to help them really to understand their Bible better, for there was no one who understood it too well. He might say that his travels in the East, which, by the kind permission of his Church be enjoyed last spring, had practically made the Bible a new book to him, and if he could help other people to understand it a little better through his travels and experiences in the East, he shold be delighted that he had come there. Everyone knew that the Bible, though lb was dedicated to all races and conditions ef people, was nevertheless an Oriental Book. Its incidents and its manners and customs were Oriental, and they must have some know- ledge of Oriental life to understand it. He than pro- ceeded to describe the costunaes of the gentlemen on the platfoten, the first one being av Eastern Sheik. fie said it was almost certain that Jesus Christ was dressed similarly to their friend before them. The outfit of the rich man was then dealt with, the Lscturer remarking that the treasure of the rich man of the East consisted largely in the extent of his ward- robe. In modern times rich men had been found with ae many as 200 different suits. The lecturer described at considerable length, the costume of the Easton, peasant and then referted to the shopkeeper. He said the Eastern shopkeeper was a study. He was never in a hurry. He sat in his bazaar which was similar to a big square supbosed, smoaing, and did not ask anyone to buy till they asked him the price of an article. He would then ask a very much higher price than he thought people would pay, for instance he would ask £2 10s. for an article and eventually come down to 15s. An interesting curiosity was the shopkeepers purse which was a very fancy article. It had tassels which the owner fastened to his girdle. An Egyptian runner was the next character dealt with. The lecturer observed ' that all men in the Best wore girdles, their garments making them a necessity. leome of them were of great value, being made of the richest silk that could possibly be produced. Mohammedans wore silken girdles although they were forbidden to do so by Mohammedan law. The costumes of the ladies weze then referred to, and the lecturer described a wedding at Jerusalem, which was enacted as described in the parable of be ten bridesmaids. He spoke of the belief of the people in charms,and said they had no real faith in God. They were utterly and absolutely superstitious. His travels in the East had confirmed hit faith as a Pretestant minister ;he was a Proteetant be- fore, but he was a thousand times more a Protestant now. CApplatufe.) He had learned during his travels in the East that the greatest curse with which humanity nag afflicted to-day was the priest. W hen he went to Jsrtralern aid went in the sacred temples and heard the paltry nonsense that the priests taught there, when be saw the priest watching as the poor belated victims of superstition came up and kissed sacred pictures and afterwards knelt down and kissed a den°, when he saw priests walkieg about the streets,and wemen up his hands and kissing them, he felt the curse of humanity was the priest. Lie poisoned religion at its fountain head, he poisoned life at it fountain head, and the curse of curses was he. (Applause.) After exp!ain- hsg several pictures of scenes in the East. the lecturer comcluded by thanking the audience for their patient hearing. (Applause.) Tee Rev. leutonome BISHOP proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer. He said it was quite irnpoesible to find words in which to sufficiently express their grateful thanks te Mr. Lamb for his ietersstine and instructive lecture. Many of them would understand the Scriptures better for having heard his description of the manners and customs of the East. The motion was cariied with acclamation. A similar compliment haring been pail te the Chair- man, the proceedings termicated with the singing of the Doxology.
Ebe " Crammer "

St. Paul's.

The Rev. E. R. Tarbuck in the course of his sermon on Sunday evening said there was a most sicPnificaut condition running through all their petitions and it was essential that they should note that condition. The con- dition was that the issue of the war might be to God's honour and glory and the goad of man. If it be neces- sary for the glory of God or the good of man that they should be the losers, then God's will be done and they must abide by the decision of their omniscient lz:rd. It, for instance, they had, as foreign nations said they had, become cenreited and overbearing, or if they had neg, lected to do justice to other nations, or if society in Eng- land had become very irreligious, very disloyal to God, or very immoral, then it might be necessary for the dignity of God and the good of man that they should receive some great national reverse. Now England, rightly, or otherwise, believed that we should not have accepted the challenge of the enemy if we as a nation had not felt that it was morally necessary. And so they prayed for victory believing that their cause was just in Gcd's eyes, and yet expressing our willingness to abide by the decision of Him who showeth all things. Holy Trinity Church.
Dinner to the Sergeants of the sth Irish Service Company. No Discontent at Warrington.

On Saturdsy evening,at their headquarters,in Everton brow, Liverpool, the 5% Irish V.B.K L.R. gave a duane to the sergeants of the special company for service in South Africa, whose names ere Messrs. J Berisford (sergeant-instructor), J Shields, T Carr, T Callaghan, W Smith, an W M'Donnell. Sergeant-Major M'Dannell presided, and there was an attendance of about 40. The loyal toasts having been honoured, Quartermaster- Sergeant G. Donnelly proposed that of "The &.rgeants of the Service Company."—Sergeant Instructor Beriaford responded, and referred to the rumours which had been spread about that the men had ben discontented whilst at Warrington, but he was glad to say that they were false, and that the men had behaved splendidly. (Applause.)
Private E. Jones, of Warrington.
ONE OF THE SOUTH LANCASHIRES KILLED AT SPION KOP.

The above is taken from a photograph of the late Private Ellis Jones, a reservist of the let South Lancashire Regiment, who previously resided at Warrington and who was killed in the recent en- gagement at Spion Kop. The deceased who was twenty five years of age had not been in service abroad before the present war. His wife lives in Rose-yard, off Dial-street, Warrington, and feels her loss keenly. She had received several affection- ate letters from her husband.

The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, preaching at Holy Trinity Church on Sunday morning, said he doubtel not that God would bring us safely through the crisis; but even so, our self-confidence had received a rude shock. We had been made to feel how the most esalced earthly greatness might be speedily brought down, and how in the mysterious providence of God earthly powers and earthly enapires could in a moment be made to totter to their fall. Any greatness that we enjoyed as a nation, and any prosperity that we enjoyed as individuals, they must remember while thankful for it, that it conferred responsibility, It was not a thing to be vain of, bat a thing to be regarded as a trust for the benefit of otherscand if our aims were altogether nelfish in the war they would not prosper ; if it was simply our own gain, our own aggandizement, our own vanity, that was the ruling motive in the action vie had taken, then we could hardly expeet God to bless our efforts ; but if we were indeed seeking to aid the oppressed, ar.d to ameliorate the condition of the down-trodden, and to bring Smith Africa within the civilizing influences of Christian freedom, and a free institution with a view to their own benefit aa well as that of the world at large, then they might ask Heaven to help them in the work thoy had in baud. Thoir duty was a•duty of repentence of. their sins. There had been sin sufficient in this land of ours to call down upon us His judgment; there had been eloneh of selfish indulgence,forgetfulness of God,neglect of His worship, Sabbath breaking, gambling, vanity, and immorality in every shape and form.
