div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS. LORD ROBERTS' ADVANCE.
Brilliant Move by General French. Five Boer Laagers Captured.

Lord Roberts has at last begun his advance. That was the great news of yesterday, and happily there is every reason to hope that the encouraging feeling which the knowledge must awaken in every true English heart will not be damped by any serious reverse of fortune. The real operations began on the 11th, when Colonel Hannay, in command of a brigade of mounted infantry, marched from Orange River to Ram Dam, a place probe- bably on the left bank of the Riet River, a few miles above Jacohadal, and secured the right flank wf the ad- vance against a Beer attack, at the same time screening the march of the column from Boar scouts. Then.on the 12th, French, with his cavalry division, seized the river crossing at Dekil's Drift, on the east bank of which, and therefore across the Riot River, the Sixth and Seventh Divisions are now ' encamped, the latter being that of General Tucker. On the 13th, French, with three brigades of Cavalry,. Horse Artillery, and a strong force of Mounted Infantry, made a further advance to Klip Drift, on the Madder River, well to Cronje's left fink where he forced a passage, and occu- pied the hills to the north, capturing three laagers, with supplies. At the same time he detached Colonel Gordon with a cavalry brigade, who seized Bondeval Drift, four miles to the west, and a third drift b?tween Eondeval and Blip Drifts, with two laagers. On Tuesday night the Sixth Division -was on the north bank of the Riot and marching to support the Cavalry, and the Seventh was to follow en Wednesday afternoon.

div.head: FLYING COLUMN IN ZULULAND,
div.p: THE FLYING COLUMN IN ZULULAND,
"In Splendid Fighting Form."
Arrival at Eshowe
DURBAN, FEBRUARY 13, 2.10 P.M.

The column of Colonial Scouts sent into Zululand are at present guarding Eshowe, having executed a forced march from North Zululand. Tao column had some rough experiercee on thp journey, and were most glad of the rest afforded on their arrival at the capital. The scouts received a cordial welcome at Eshowe, and were liberally entertained by the inhabitants. The men were highly pleased with the manceuvring of Vieir commander, Colonel Addison, and although the column was surrounded by the Boers two or three times ia the course of the journey Colonel Addison ekilfully brought his men out of the difficulty. The column is in splendid fighting form, and has been twice at leandlwarsa. The last time they left just before Noata was captured. The. police there made a brave stand and killed three Boers and only surrendered when shelled by big guns. The Boers pursued the column for a considerable distance when the latter was retiring on Eshowe, but desisted when patrolling parties were sent out in order to draw them into an ambuscade.

div.head: SOLDIERS WISHING THEY WERE DEAD.
div.p: SOLDIERS WISHING THEY WERE DEAD.
Letter trom Lance-Corporal O'Nei
of Runcorn.

The following letter has been received by the father of Lance-Corporal O'Neil, of Runcorn, now out with the South Lancashire Regiment at South Africa :—" Dear Father,—l write you these few lines hoping to find you in good health as the parting of this letter leaves me. Thank God for it dear father we are now on our road to Ladysmith. We have been marching since Tuesday morning, day 'and night, under the burning sun. It would roast you here in the day ; whilst. at night it comes down as hard as • it can with rain. We are now having a day's rest at Springfield, and leave to-morrow for 20 miles march into Ladysmith. When we were marching through Preston and Liverpool you could hear people say : " I wish we could come." Well if they had they would wish themselves back again, for we have to go through rivers and everything we come to. If some of the young men of Runcorn had to go through what we are going through they would wish them9elves dead. Its not" come home and get yourself dry "when you are wet through. Dear father you should be out here. It would not be : "Get me a pint for dinner and another for tea !" You would be sati,fled if you got water. We get one biscuit and a drink of water. We havn't had our clothes off since we loft Ragland. We are only too glad to drop down anywhere and sleep. You can hear fellows say "I wish I was dead "or "some Boers &me and shoot us dead we would be out of our misery then." You talk about the Crimean war its nothing to this. Good night and God bless y oc,from your son Lance-Corporal O'Neil.

div.head: Another Letter from Private Spencer, of Runcorn.
div.p: Another Letter from Private Spencer, of Runcorn.

The following letter has been received from Private W. Spencer. of the South Lancashire Regimen; by his wife. Speacer, it will be remembered, was missing after the Spion Kop disaster. In answer to inquiries made by his wife at the War Office, they intimate they have no knowledge as to what has become of him. 12 January, 1900.—Dear Wife,—Just a few lines to let you know how we are getting on. We are having terrible hard times of it now. We left Estcourt on the 9th of January, at 5 o'clock in the morning, and were marching all night until 5 o'clock, through a drenching rain. We had to sleep in our wet things, and let them dry on us, as we had only one suit of clothes with us We set off again next day, under a burning sun, to take the Boers in front of U 3. When they saw us they went away, and we followed them up. They were going towards Ladysmith, and we were only two days' march from Ladysmith. The wors day we had was the 10th. Marching under a burning sun we hid nothing but one biscuit and same bully beef for about 24 hours and could get no water. The water we do get is like clay water. The men were falling nut like rottese sheep and we were getting fagged up. We have had no money for a fortnight and we can get no more till the war is over. You can show this to Harry Moores if you like. Give my best respects and love to mother and all the rest.
Your hving husband Bill,
P.S.—This is the last of the writing paper." Intercession Services at Runcorn.

By direction of the Bishep of Ch...4ter, special services of intercession on behalf of her Majesty's naval and military forces engaged in South Africa were held at the Established Churches in Runcorn and distaict on Sun- day. The form of service consisted of portions of the Litany, with supplementary clauses, and special collects and prayers. Proper psalms and hymns were a'so used. At the Parish Church, in the mornir,g, the pulpit was occupied by the Vicar (Rev. Canon Maitland Wood),and at evensong the preacher was the Rev. W. H. Stables. senior curate. At Holy Trinity Church, in the morning, the Litany and special prayers were read by the Vicar (Rev. C. R. Billiok), who also preached the sermon. Jo Zhe evening, the service was conducted by the Ilcv N .1 Poole (curate), farad the choir sang the special hymn com- posed by the Rev W H Draper,and set to music by John E West. entitled " Lord, hear Thy people's prover, for those who fight in liberty's great name." Similar ser- vices were h-Id at St. Michael's (All Angels), Runcorn, and St. John the Evangelist, Weston.

div.head: Another Warrington Man Killed at Spion Kop.
div.p: Another Warrington Man Killed at Spion Kop.

News has just been received by Mrs. Rater, of Folly lane, Warrington,of the death of her brother, Private W Lloyd, a reservist,of the 2nd Battalion Royal Lancasters, who has died from wounds received at Spion Lop He had seen service in many places abroad. He left Aldershot for India, where he remained two years, and then he went to South Africa at the time of the Jameson Raid, sailing on the as. Victoria, along with Jameson, to Malta. There be joined the other battalion for two years, and sailed for China. Wh,!e there he volunteered for police duty in the plague-stricken parts of Hong-Kong. Thence he was seat to Singapore, and finished his time last March,returning home in April. He was a great lover of sport, and assisted his regiment on different occasions, playing for the Lancaster° when they won the Northern Indian-Army Shield. He was em- ployed at the Jockey-lane Loco. Department, and he left Warrington on November 20th, to "do or die for Queen and country."

div.head: DEPARTURE OF MORE WARRING TON AMBULANCE MEN.
div.p: DEPARTURE OF MORE WARRING TON AMBULANCE MEN.
Hearty 'Send-off."

As we stated in our last issue, six members of the Warrington Corps of the St. John Arabslance Brigade— Superintendent Buckley and Privatos J. T. Dimelow, J, Maddock, W. Johnson, W. E. L Nagmore. and E. G. Kelly, have been sele2ted for service in South Africa. Private Dimelow lett Warrington for London on Tuesday night, where be will undergo a course of training pre- paratory to being despatched to the front, and the other members se!ected laowed on Wednesday night. On Tue4day evening a smoking concert was held at the Pelican Inn, Butterrnarket-street, by way of a'hearty " send-off" to the men. Captain Waring presided, and after the toast of " :he Queen" had been enthusiaitic- ally honoured, he read several apologies for non-attend- ance. Mr. Robert Pierpoint, M.P, telegraphed from the House of Commons Sorry unable to be with you. Give Diraelow my host wishes. We must all feel proud of oar men's readiness to serve in South Africa."

The Mayor (Alderman Robers) wrote—::—" Dear Captain Waring, lam sorry I shall not be with you this evening. Please convey to Mr. Dirnelow my warm con- gratulation upon his patriotic spirit in offering hims4f for ambulance work in South 4.trica. We have already witnessed on other occasions how devoted the spirit of Warrington men is in the present critical time but it is most gratifying that although the struggle which is now going on is more protracted than anybody anticipated a few months ago the same determined spirit to overcome all obstacles at any cost, obtains. Wishing Dimelow a safe voyage, a successful time and a speedy return and with the best wishes for the continued success of your corps, believe me, yours faithfully, H. ROBERTS" Mr. J. Charlton Parr sent a cheque ter £4 which was divided among the men and a reservist named Baguley a membor of the corps. Cholera belts were sent for presentation to the men by the Misses Turner, Balaclava caps from Mr. T. J. Logb, tobacco from Mr. C. Chalmers, and matches from Mr. Toft. Mr. H. Cooke (station master at Bank Quay) regretted his inability to be present. Captain Waring presented the gifts to the men on be- half of the donors. During the course of his remarks he said he was slue the mni did them great credit. He believed there were only three supernumerary officers selected to go to the front out of the whole of tbe ambul- ance corps in the Unite i Kingdom, and he was pleased to say they had one in Superintendent Buckley. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Buckley was one of the first men who helped to form the Corps. He had hoard from Holloway, Newns and Malkin, and they were vary well and liked it very much. Holloway was at a hospital just outside Capetown. -

_ . r. G. P. CROSFIELD, 9n proposing the health ot th- Prince of Wales,the Grand Prior of the Order ot St. John of Jerusalem and of the St. John Ambulance,Brigade said ha was sure there was no member of the Brigade who was prouder ot the way ia which th 3 men had volun- teered for service on the occasion of this war, than the Prince hinvelf. (Hear,hear.)He (Mr. Crosfield) would have been very sorry to have missed that opvrtunity of wishing " God-speed " to the men in the corps who were going out. It gave him the greatest pleasure to think they were sending six men. Other corps had been seed- ing out large numbers lately and he was beg:nning to he a little afraid that the Warrington c-)ros was goinz to be " left out "a bit. That was not so, t owevar, as altogether they had sent nine man, which he then tv, was most creditable considering the numbers they had in uniform. Th9re was one little bit of advice he woOd like to give those who were going out. He was sure each one of them would b 3 a credit to the bigaie, te the Warrington corps and to old Warrington. With r rgard to the ambulance work probably many things would crop up which they had not learnt in the bock. What they had got to do was tn tiFe their common s3nse. He now ask,nl them to drink the health of the Prince of Wales. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with enthusiasm.

Dr. ADAMS proposed the heath ol the departing gu's's. He said it was a matter of poraonal pride to think toat most of the men who were going out were to iar,et extent his own creations in that branch of work. Wt-iile he was proud thny were going out he was sorry to think they were leaving them. He wished them bon voyage, successful service, and a speedy r3turn. It was a credit to Warrington that they htd sent so many men to the front and had still more to send if the authorities called upon then, to do so. Superintendent BUCKLEY briefly responclei. During the owning scveral musical items and recita- tions were given and were much appreciated.

div.head: Sir J. T. Brunner and the War.
div.p: Sir J. T. Brunner and the War.

At the annual meeting of the Everton Liberal Associa- tion on Monday evening a communication was read from Sir John Brunner. M.P., the president of the asssciation, expressine regre.-. at his absence. Referring to the war, he wrote that the discussinn as to whether the war was a just one or rot appeared to him to be a very barren one, but in hi 3 opinion it was one out of which nothing short of a miracle could produce any good to anyone. The Boer Government was undoubtedly corrupt, but whether a Government of mineowners would be much better in other respects he greatly doubted. If herea e'er the mineowners ruled supreme in Johan- nesbarg, they would emnloy far fewer Enelista- mei and far more llaffrs than heretofore le for that smaller number of English miners the places would be no Paradise. We would distrust even employers in England if they had supreme control of an English town, but in South Africa, without trades unions, without indep-ndent newspapers, Sze., a set of emp'oyers, cnnsisting mainly of international financier., would attsuredly develop for Englishmen as well as for Kaffir. a system of virtual s'avery. As to the taxpayers in England, looking to the certainty of the terrible cost of the war having to be met, to the equal certainty that we would have to maintain a large army in South Mica, ard to the taQt that the German Emperor had

div.head: Letter from an Earlestown Man.
div.p: Letter from an Earlestown Man.

Corporal Ben Tripp, South Lancashire Regiment, in a letter, under date of the 13:h ult., to his mother in Earlestown, states :—" Tbelwhole of our division (Fifth Division) left Estcourt for march en route on the 9,11, and I shall never forget the sight as long as I live. We struck camp at 3 a.m.,and were off by 6 a.m. in torrents of rain. It was the most trying march I ever did. We went twelve miles in twelve hours ; so you can imagine the state of the roads. We were up to our knees in mud, and we had to go through rivers, streams, and swamps almost up to our waists. We had only one suit of clothes each, so that they had to dry on us. Next day we were uff again to Frere Camp. This day was the reverse of the previous day. It was dry and dusty and extremely hot, and when we got in Frere Camp we were all done up, hungry and thirsty. I was lucky in meet- ing a very old c3rpeade whe was with me in Warring- ton, and whom I bad not seen since I left Jersey. He left the 40th Rgiment in 1892 to join the Army Service Corps as a baker. Next morning found us on the march again, and that night we got blocked by a river, and so had to halt for about two hours. It had been raining,and the roads were fearfully muddy; but in spite of that we lay down on the mud and slept soundly. At day- break all were ready to proceed. We waded through the river, and. reached Springfield just in time to turn the Boers, and prevent them train blowing up Spring- field Bridge. We are now about twenty miles west of Colenso, and twenty miles from Ladysmith, thing a flanking movement on the Boers' extreme right. We are on the eve of battle, and are all very anxi me to meet the Boers. I ana with the Maxim gun as range finder. Myself and another corporal take the exact range for the gun to fire, and then get under cover and fire away at the enemy as we like. I conld write for a week of the diff,rent events which occurred during the march, but time is precious. We get together in twos and threes, and co3k for ourselves' Bully-beef, biscuits, and tea is our diet. We break the biscuits in piecereand mince the bully-beef, and boil the lot together; our fireplace being anthills. These hills are about 2ft. high. We cut a hole in the middle, one in front, and another behind, s 3 that the wind can get at it. We then make places for our mess tins en the top, and cook our food in thia manner. We have not got our chocolate yet ; but we have plenty of tobacco. Copree mixture was the last we received. We are a happy lot ; singing and cheering all day love, and making the best of things. I will write after the first battle—our baptism of fire, We hope to relieve Lad/smith in a day or two at the most. Tell father I met a brother of Jim Worsleys, the striker, he is with our brigade in the Lancaster Regiment, also a chap by the name of Harrop. He used to go to scheol with me, his regiment is the Lancashire Fusilier, and he 19 with our brigade also,his father used to be a keeper for Mr. Harwood.

div.head: St. Helens Man at the Tugela.
div.p: A St. Helens Man at the Tugela.

Private T. Farneu, I Company of the Ist South Lancashire Regimeot of the Natal Field Force, writing to his mother at 71, Hamer-street, St. Helens, from Soringfield Camp, Tugela River, under date January 15, 1900, says :—" We have been on the march nearly night and thy; the first day from Estcourt to Frere, from half-past four in the morning until six at night, up hills three parts of the way,and up to our knees in mud. We had to wait six hours at one river, it being in flood, pouring rain all the time, and when we did cross seven rlfle were washed away, and horses and men nearly drowned. We left the next day. It was roasting hot, and went about six miles, then rested till dark, had a drink of mud and started off again. The troops kept falling into ho'es in the road. It was a fearful march for about three hours, with dead horses on the road, traction engines capsizing, and there was great corn- metion among the mules and bullocks. There was an- other river to cros, but we couldn't gat any wetter. In we went, and got on another couple of miles. We could not get across the other river, ane had to wait for the engineers to bridge it; so we lay down in the mud and rkin till daylight. When we crossed the river we had to go up a long hill to Pretorius Camp. We stayed four hours, and then had a race for a bridge over the little Tugela River. Th Lancers had a skirmish with about 200 Boers, with the result that two officers were wounded. The Lancers retired,and we came up,and the Boers disappeared. Hundreds of the men fell out, clean done up. We are now four and a half miles from the "fugela River, which the Boers bold in force. The Fre" State Boers are opposite us. We have had nothing but biscuit and tinned beef for a week."
Intercession Services at Warrington.

In aceordance with the recomnaendatioa of the Arch- bishops of Canterbury and York, &mdsy was set apart as a day of intercession and supplicatioa on behalf of our trove in South Africa, in the Church of England throughout the coentry. Warrington Parish Church. Speciel services were held at the Warrington Parish Church, and it had been arranged that the Mayor and Corporation should attend the morning service. Owing to the heavy fall of snow on Saturday night, which rendered the streets almost impassable a fresh circular was sent to eech member of the Council intimating that the procesiion would be abandoned. The attendance at the church was much smaller than it has been for some time. All the clergy were present, and Mr. W. S. Woods was at the organ. The special Psalm which was selected was ec:vi., the first two verses being " God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea." The Litany was taken from the " Memorial Ser- vice" for those who have fallen in the war, as used at St. Paul's Cathedral, on December 19.;h 1899. The hymns were 83, 525, 259, 322, mid 315, and the mulic of the choral celebration was taken from Dyke's and fderbeck's settings. The preacher was the Rev. A S Cameron who, in the mrse of a short address, said it, was his duty and his privilege to endeavour to say one or twowords that might lead teeir thoughts in the direction of fervent, earnest and intense prayer to God for their cause. If their Lord's words about prayer were truP,the most powerful men were the men of prayer. " Whatsoever ye shall ask ths Fither in My name He will give it you." Nothing ever succeeded in this world in the true meaning of the word succees, without being prayed for. Did they not forget all that when they eutered so lightly on the pre- sent great struggle? They exulted in their enormous strength, and imaeined that the whole world was lying at their feet. They wete boasttul, some even brav,att: and blustPrinZ, but God was showing us that the b 7ttlo was not alwaye to the strong, for they had been baffled and check d and had reverses which a few weeks ag ) they would have imagined utt, rly impossible. Of course they knew the empire had great streneth, and tee struggle was showing where the inexhaustible mine of strength was in the loyalty and bravery, enthusi)4rn awl patriotiene of the sons of the empire, but G idwoete net let them use that strength exeent in humble trust, faith and loviag deh•neence upon Film. Trilt they had f ergett-n, and they had to learn the old old lesson in the old old way. At the evening service the Rector pointed out the undoubted serionines3 of the present position, but at the same tiffi the absence of all cause for alarm, show- ing telt wader the circumstances the course adopted was nr thabl v the best, and that failure in the measures now ,ttempt.(l would not affect the ultimata issue ;that they w Ire.in the hands of capable and competent leaders with immense resourcos, supported by a united nation and enthusiastically loyal colonies. But the chief ground of confi leace lay in this, that the cause was just, and for these great reasons : first, that the land was theirs by a title of a hundred years ; secondly, that the Government was for the benefit of the people, on the testimony ef the most impartial residents ; thirdly, that the possession of South A rice was for the good of the world ; and,lastly, that in their belief their acciaisitiea was for the hence ir and glory of God, that His name and will might be spread by us among Veil nations of the world. St. James', Latchford. The Rev. F. E. Powell, vicar, eaid that if they desired to hold the position the p-ovidence of God had given to their great and wonderful Eespire, they must connect the love of country with the love of God. Religion and patriotism moat go hand in hand, or their glory would be taken away and given to another. He confessed an utter inability to understand the position of these who said that the war was a national crime and a diserace and yet who refused to urge its immediate cessation' If it was wrong to commence the war, it was wrong to continue it; and whatever finite theie might have been on their side in the conduct of aff )irs they believed the Government was honest when it said it never desired war nor thought it pessible until subsequent evente proved thlt it was, unhejepily. inevitable. Had the Beers without equivocation consented to treat the British in the Transvaal as the British in South Africe treated the Dutch, there could have been no war. Upon the Boers, then, must chiefly ret the awful reip<msi- bility of the war, although they might well believe that

div.head: Send-off to a Volunteer.
div.p: Send-off to a Volunteer.

A smoking conaert was held the other evening at the Marquis of Granby by about fifty of the National Ass- elation of Operative Plasterers (Warrington District) and their labourers for the purpose of mqking a presentation and wishing God speed to Will.am Heesom, who is one of their members, and who has volunteered for the front. The chair was taken at eight o'clock by Mr. T. Oxley,. and songs were rendered by Messrs. Lomax, Frangleton, Clare, Oxley, Burns, and H. Heesom, and the usual toasts were drunk.—Mr. William Sixsmith, in making the presentation, briefly spoke of the good feeling which existed amongst all those present, and hoped the recipient would soon be back amongst them.—Mr. William Heeeom briefly respended, and a he- rty vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman and CommiLtees, also to the hostess, Mrs. Whittle, and the proceedings were brought to a clone by the singing :of the National Anthem. The pre3ent consisted of a purse of gold, pipe and tobacco.

The weekly meeting of the Earlestown and Dis- - P.SA.. Seciety was held in the Co-operative Hall on Sunday afternoon. Mr E Kenyon presiaed and the principal speaker was Mr G Burgess of Talford. Vocal selections were given by Mr. Twemlow and the Male Quartette party.

div.head: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS.
div.p: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS.

On Sunday the annual services in connection with the Wesleyan Home Missions were held in the Wesleyan Chapel, Barlestown The sermons were preached by the Rev. G. W. Lunn of Prescot. On Monday evening the annual meecing was held in the chapel, when Dr. Thompson presided. The Res. P. R. Pa smote read the annual general report,ani an address was given by the Rev. C. W. Andrews of Bolton. Collections were made in aid of the Mis- t.ion funds.
•'!7;;;.&" FIRIs AT NEWTON.

On Monday—morning about 2 O'clock a wooden shed behind the Pied Bull Rote' Newton, was dis- covered to be on fire. The premises are owned by Mr. A W Bishop and the fire was discovered by John Barnley whose house adjoins the back premises of the Hotel. He immediately informed Mr. Bishop and buckets of water were thrown on the flames but without any effect and by 2.30 a.m, the shed was burned to the ground. The shed con- tained a small quantity of bay and provender and some farm implements. The damage which was edtimated at £3O is not insured. SUDDEN DEATH AT EARLESTWN.

The death of Mary Wright wife of George Wright which took place suddenly at her residence,s,Sef ton- street, Newton Common has been reported to the Harlestown police. The deceased, who was 43 years of age, was attended 12 months ago by Dr. Latham of Eeriest° wn, but has not since hai any medical attendance. During the night of Monday deceased's husband had to get up and attend to her several times, and at about 8-30 a.m. on Tuesday he got up to make her a cup of tea. On taking the tea up- stairs he found deceased lying unconscious on the room floor. Dr. Latham was immediately sent for and he arrived as deceased was dying. Death occurred at 11-15 a.m, on fuesday morning. Dr. Latham expressed the opinion that the cause of death was influenza, on a weak constitution. FUNERAL OB THE LATE MR. ISAAC BATEMAN. The remains of the late Mr. Isaac Bateman,whose death we reported last week, were interred at the Varlestown Cemetery on Saturday afternoon. The weather was most inclement, snow falling fast during the whole of the afternoon,which prevented many who would have liked to pay a last tribute of tespect to the deceased, from being present. A small number of Freemasons of the Makerfield Lodge however, braved the elements,and several members of Messrs M'Corquodale and Company's office staff, also attended. Amongst the relations present were Mr John Sloe, Mr W Attfield, Mr J Walkden, and three nephews. The body was borne to the grave by four sergeants belonging to the Newton Company of the 6th V. 8., with which Mr Bateman vele con- nected. The service was performed by the Rev J Ryder, vicar of Newton, and as the Masons filed past the grave they dropped sprigs of acacia on the coffin. Several floral wreaths were sent by Colonel Wood, the office staff, relatives, wife and family,Mr and Mrs Cutts, and Mr J Simkins.

ALARMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT EARLESTOWN, An alarming accident, which was brtunately at- tended with no serious consequences occurred at Earlestown Junction on Saturday morning. The train due at Warrinwon at half-past nine from St. Helens had just arrived at Earlestown, and whilst the passengers were alighting a light engine, which was proceeding for water to Parkside, Newton-le- Willows, on the Manchester line, through a mis- management of the points,ran on to the Warrington line. The driver failed to perceive until too late that he was on the wrong line, and the engine dashed into the Warrington train. A large milkvan was in the rear. The impact derailed and smaghed to atoms the hinder part of the van, and a buffer of the engine was also destroyed. The carriages in the centre of the train were buffer-locked, but, be- yond a slight shaking to the pa-,sengera, no further damage was done. The guard's van was next to the milkvan, but, fortunately,the guard was on the platform at the time; under other ciacumstances he could not have escaped a vary serious accident. The stationmaster and his employees speedily got to work, and the wreckage was removed within half an hour of the collision.

div.head: 'WARRINGTON A COUNTY BOROUGH.
div.p: 'WARRINGTON A COUNTY BOROUGH.
Inquiry at the Town Hall.

Colonel W. Langton Coke,M. I.nst.,C.E. conducted an inquiry at the Town Hall, Warrington, on Thurs- day, into the representation of the -Corporation to become a County Borough. The Corporation was represented by Mr. J K Bradbury(instracted by the Town Clerk). Mr. Wilson, solicitor of the County Offices, Preston, appeared on behalf of the Lanca- shire County Council. There were also the Mayor (Alderman Roberts), Councillors Bennett. John Evans, Peacock, Shillcock, Rogers; Mr. J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Mr. John Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Mr. Th9mas Longdin(borough surveyor), Dr. Gornall (medical officer of health), Mr. W H Woodcock (borough collector and assistant over- seer), Mr. James Deus (water engineer), Mr. C Madeley (librarian), and Messrs. John Harrison and S Gough and Ewart. COUNSEL'S OPENING eTATENENT. Mr BRADBURY in stating the case for the CerPoration, said he was glad to inform the Inspector that the appli- cation was supported by the unanimoas vote of the Town Council. There was no oppestion,the feeling toeing that:the time had certainly come when Warringtonishould have its proper place as one of the county boroughs of the country.He did not propose to go deeply into the his- tory of the borough. No doubt it would be very interest- ing to the townspeople, but he thought considering how the case stood, it should be scarcely necessary to do thatl Be would say shortly how the borough stood. It was incorporated by charter in 1847, and at that time the borough was situated partly in the county of Chsshire and partly in the county of Lancaster. In 1854 the Warrington Improvement Act was pissed, and it incor- porated the Towns Improvement Clauses Act, the Police Clauses Act, and the Markets and Fairs Clauses Aet. The townships at that time in the borough were as follows :—The urban township of Warrington, part of the township of Latchford, and part of the town- ship of Thelwall. Tue Werrington township was in Lancashire and the parts of the other two townships in Cheshire. By the Union of Parishes Act, Thelwall was added to part of Latchford, and that became one town- ship under the name of Latchford. In 1898 tae Latch- ford township was added to Warrington, and the whole of the borough therefore became one township—the township of Warrington. He had said that part of the borough was in Cheshire, the parts of Letcnford and Thelwall. The Local Government Act, 1888, provided that where a borough was sitnated partly in one county and partly in another, upon the Act corning into , force the borough would be altogether in that county which contained the largest nutnber of the inhabitants of thel borough. That was to say that if the preponderant portion were in Lancashire, the Act provided that the whole of the borough shall be ie Lancashire. In that way the portions of Latchford and Thel wall formeely in Chsshiro became trateferred to 'Lan- cashire, and the whole of the borough is at that time constituted became in the county of Lancashire. In 1890 the borough was slightly exteeded upon the north side. Most of that poreine, not piptileus, was north of the Cheshire Lines Railway. In 1896 a very important extension took ola.ce cc the southerly side. The Extension Order was made iu 1896. Tire effect of it was that a numner of totieships at part of townshipi were added to the borough. He read paragraph three of the Corporation's memorial to the Local Government Board : "That in the year 1896 unaer a Provisional order of your Right Honourable Board, coefirmed by the Local Government Board's Provisional Orders Confirm e- tion (Warrington) Act, 1896, the beundary of the boroueh was extended so as to include, in addition to the area of the then existing borough the township of Little Sankey and parts of the townships of Appleton- with-Hull, Latchford Without, Walton Inferior, and Poulton-with-Fearnhead, comprising an era of 1,111 acres with an estimated population of 2,826." On the southerly side that brought the boundary of the borough to the river and on the south-easterly side to the Ship Canal. The river being the boundary for the two counties they went over the boundary an; included in the borough that portion of Cheshire between the river and the Ship Canal. The Order provided that the whole of the borough was to be ia the county of Lancaster, and the effect was that the portion of Cheshire referred to was transferred to Lancashire. The position that brought them to was that Warrington was one township and was in the county of Lancaster, the southerly leounda.ry be- ing the river and the ship canal. Of course the impor- tant point in this application was the question of popu- lation. . lie need scarcely say to the inspector that a csrtain population was a sine qua non. If there was such a population, unless there were special reasons against it, the Local Government Board would advise an order to be made. The Inspector would see by the memorial that in 1891 the population of Warrington was 52,742, which, of course, in itself was more than the Act required. The INSPECTOR: Fifty thousand. Mr. BRADBURY : Ye:?. Continuing, he said their estimate of the mumber of popuiatien per house in 1891 came out about 5.5. As he had said, there had since been an extension, weich had added considerably to the area of the borough. When the case was being prepared in regard to the extension the figures were worked out for the population in April of 1895. The number of houses in the borough in occupation were actually counted, and the population was estimated at five per house. That was less than the figure in the first case. That worked out to a population of 57,000. With the added area in 1896 the. extra population was estimated at 2,826. They had also to add the increase in the population from April 1895 to the end of 1899. The Borough Surveyor hal taken the number of new ()ousel built in the borough More that 'period, and it canoe to 1,906 He had also satisfied himself that the number of empty houtes at the present time Was considerably less than it was when he made his previous calculation. The question of empty houses was therefore excluded. Be said, however, that owing to public improvements 50 houses had been pulled down since 1895 which must come from the total. 1.908. That left the addition of occupied houses since April, 1895, 1,866. Taking the ratio of five to each house that worked out to 9,330. Mr. BRADBURY said that with regard to the borough's indebtedness the total liability on March 31st last, in - chiding the debt of the gas and water undertakings and tee capitalized value of the annuities charge on those undertakings amounted to £539,271, made up as follows :—Borough rata, £30,023 improve- ment rate £70,060 ; general sewers rate, £84,281; gas undertaking, £183,792; and water undertaking, £271,115. From the two last-named undertakings there was provided after paying the interest and sinking fund, a considerable profit to the borough. The real indebtedness of the borough was £134,000,and roughly speaking the ratable value was £222,000. The amount of indebtedness, therefore, was only twolth"rds of the ratable value. As the Inspector was aware, a borough was entitled to barrow twice the amount of its ratable value, and the Warrington Corporation would be entitled to borrow £44,000. They had only borrowed 2134,000. Mr. loomensm was then called. He said that he had been the Borough Surveyor of Warrington since 1878. The town had grown very rapidly,particularly so during the last five years. He proceeded to refer to the con- ditions of Arpley meadows up to 1892 speaking of the bad approaches thereto and the flolding which took place. He detailed the improvements which had re- cently been carried out by the London and North- Western Railway Company. The Corperatien had con- tribeted the sum of £2,120 for the widening of the bridge over the railway, and the land owners had given the land for the roads: Arplev meadows were now thoroughly developed and contained 363 acres which could be opened up for building purposes. Since the construction of the Snip Canal the flooding difficulty had been removed. Negotiations were at the present time being conducted with the owners by several firms for 50 acres of land for the erection of works. (A letter in confirmation of this statement was read from Messrs. J. White, Mclver and Company, estate agents, who owned 192 out of the 447 acres whieh were to be let for building purposes at the present time, He corroboratel Mr. Bradbury's state- ment that the nopula•ion of the borough at the present time was 69,156, and explained to the Inspector how he arrived at those figures. Mr. GOUGE : I should like to also ask y'cru what pro- bable change this County Borough order is likely to make in the eorough ? The BOROUGH SURVEYOR : In which way do you mean Mr Gough ? Mr GOUGE: Have we had any difficulty with the County Council in obtaining power to make roads ? The SURVEYOR that has nothing to do with my de- partment and I cannot answer it but I shall be pleased to answer you with respect to anything cencerning my department. The INSPECTOR : I .ithould think it would be better for you to put that question to the Town Clerk. The Tome CLERK 2 There has been no difficulty, Mr. GOUGE (to the Surveyor) : Can you tell me what benefit this change will bring about in the laying out of land and the building of cottages? 'The INSPECTOR:4I do not think the Borough Surveyor is in a parttime to prophecy. I cannot see how he can tell you the future. If he could he might be a very rich man. (Lane hter.) Mr. Gown( : Is it possible that the County Council would interfere in any way? The INSPECTOR: You tr-d better ask Mr. Wilson that. Mr. GOUGE: I think we ought t a know as ratepayers what the benefits of this order are. Mr. BRADBURY That is a matter ft.r the Town Council. Mr. GOUGE: The ratepayere have heard very, little as to what the financial results are likely to be. The INSPECTOR: What I have to deal with is the pe- tition of the Town Council. The point you are discus- sing ought to be thrashed out there and not before me. Mr. Genoa: I think it is desirable for you to consi- der whether this order is desirable in the interests of the ratept, yers. The INSPECTOR: That the Board will do'; but when you ask what the probable result will be I don't think

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publicatien must in al cases send their names and addresses to the Editor. Matters intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has much greater chance of insertion than a long one. The Warrington Exhibition. Sir,—Our attention has been drawn to the remarks of Mr. Councillor Bennett at a recent meeting of the Coun- cil,as reported by your eontemporary on the 7th inst. The report says " Councillor Bennett alluded to the two exhibitions which had been held in the Parr Hall, and to the annexe which it had been found necessary t I put up, A third exhibition was shortly to b 3 held, and the space between the two buildings was to be connected again." This sentence conveys an absolutely erroneous impres- sion of the facts of the case. The urge and comin )dious annexe, which has josc been competed for the forteciming Ethibition, is the first building which has over been erected for exhibition purposes on the ground in question ; both the previous exhibitions having been limited to the four walls of the Parr Hall. As t`ie prospectus issued by the promoters and many subsequent appeals for the suffrages of exhibitors and the public were based to some extent ' on this exii.eptional addition to the Exhibitioa buildings —an addition which more than doubles the area at the disposal of the Committce—we feel we ought to draw attention to an error, doubtless an unintentional one, which otherwise would reflect upon the candour and veracity of our Committee. Among other advantages gained by the addition of the annexe we have been enabled to reserve a large slice of the Parr Hall in which to construct an extensive Art Gallery, and the cordial sepport which this scheme has received from the Technical Instruction Committer of the Council, and from local and other artistei,more than Justifies this educational and interestine addition to the original plans of the promoters. Thanking you in antici- pation for inserting this letter.—Yours obediently, TIE SECItETIIIIT: 3. 75, Bridge-street, Warrington.

The Severe Weather. Warrington was visited by a severe snowstorm during Saturday night, and early on Sunday morn- ing,the streets were covered to the depth of several inches. Until about 9.30 the fall was accompanied by a sharp wind, the result being that the snow was blown about in all directions to the discomfort of pede,"rians. Mor,l severe weather has not locally been experi,mced for many years,and the result was a greatly diminished attendance at all the places of warship. A large number ot men were set to work by the Borough Surveyor, on Monday morning, in clearing away the snow, and later the public were able to walk about:the town with greater comfort and facility. GOOD TEMPLARS CONVENTION. Annual Meeting. The annual meeting of the No. 1 Convention of South West Lancashire Good Templars was held in Hope Hall, Wigan, on Saturday. There was an excellent muster, considering the very inclement weather prevailing, lodges in Earlestown, Warrington, S. Helens, Ashton, Wigan, Hiedley, Tyldesley anu Leigh being repre- sented. The Session opened at 3 45, Bro. A. Francis, C.C.T., presiding. After the opening services cred,ntial and reportiug committees were appointed. Sister le:re Duncan, P.D.S.J.T., and Sister Mrs Walker, P.D.Y.T. from Liverpool, and Bra J T Jacklin, Grand Lodge Missioner, were present as visitors. The reports of the C.C.T. and Bra E Newman C. Sec. were read, and were of an encouraging character indicating general activity. Several of the lodges reported good increases in membership. Sister Mrs Woods, C.S.J.T., eave a very satisfactory report of the juvenile section, Sister Woods regretted ttat illness had prevented her visiting all the Temples in the Coevention area. Those she had attended were doing excellent worth, and frown reports received, this seemed to be the case with others. She was pleased to report that from return; every Temple but one showed an increase in member- ship, the one exception being only reduced by 4. The membership was 715 in 10 Temples, a net increase ' 64, on the quarter, one New Temple "The Hope of Wigan "had been opened during the quarter ind now had 80 members, and was working well. It was very gratifying to learn that the juveniles had been so suc- cessful in the recent National Competitive Examination for Juvenile Templars. Out of five competing from the Pride of Earlestown Juvenile Temple, four had gained certificates. The Bloek and Gavel, gift of Bro. D. Reid D.C. Treasurer of Liverpool,had been on by the" A.E. Eccles" Temple, Ashton for largest increase on the year. Sister Mrs Walker,of Liverpool,in very impressive terms, presented the prizes to a good deputation from the suc- cessful Temple ; the S.J.T. responded. Bto George Clarke, C. Tree., reported a good balance in hand. The election of officers tor next half-year followed, the re- stilt being as folio Bro George Clarke,Earles- ' town ; C. Co. Bro I Vint, Ashton ; C.E.S, Bro C Good- all, St. Helens ; C.S.J.T. Sister Mr. Woods, Earlestown ; C V.T. Sister A Newmaa, E ttlestoeen ; C. Sec. Bro A Francis,St Helens ; C.Trea. Bro E Newman. Earlestown; C. Marshall Bro J Sheath, Warrington ; C Messenger; Sis E Sheath, Warrington ; P.C.C.P. Bro Sneaktnan.Ashton. The next Session wan fixed for Hindley on March 10th, when Bro F Bowler of Ashton is to read a paper on some suitable topic for discussion. Thanks to visitors and local friends concluded a very encouraging session. Tea followed, a large number sitting down. A very successful Public Meeting was afterwards held the Hall being crowded. An address was given by Bro. Jacklin, Mission Agent, and a musical programme was well rendered.
